# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840s–1860s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Schuylkill County was established in 1811 (per `place_search`, dateRange "+1811/"); the tools used here did not return further detail on its parent jurisdiction(s) prior to formation.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by tool output in this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States.
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for this place and period — this survey could not confirm population figures for Schuylkill County in the 1840s–1860s.
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by tool output in this survey (records below suggest a court/probate/church infrastructure typical of a settled county, but no economic data was returned).
- **Ethnic composition:** Not confirmed by tool output; the presence of a German-language Lutheran church volume (below) indicates a German-speaking population element.
- **Religious denominations:** Lutheran congregation(s) confirmed present via `volume_search` (see Church records).
- **Key historical events:** Not confirmed by tool output in this survey.

## Boundary changes
No boundary-change information was returned by the tools used in this survey. `place_search_all` was not run; if boundary history is needed, that call should be made separately.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Not stated by any page returned in this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched ("Genealogy Research Guide," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide, and "Genealogy Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) are generic overview pages, not the Pennsylvania-specific vital records page, and state only that "civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction" without giving Pennsylvania's actual date. A request to `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records` resolved to the generic "Genealogy Records" page rather than a Pennsylvania-specific article, so no registration start year/level can be cited.
- **What exists:** Not confirmed for this period from tool output.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed.
- **Gaps:** Registration start date unconfirmed — treat civil vital records for the 1840s–1860s as unverified; do not assume coverage.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Lutheran (confirmed by `volume_search`: image group 004288771, "Church Records (Lutheran)," 1840–1875, 198 images, languages English and German).
- **Record types:** Not broken out further by the tool; presumed baptisms/marriages/burials typical of Lutheran parish registers.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch-digitized volume (image group 004288771); 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — **browse-only**, and in part **German-language** (researcher must read German for at least some entries).
- **Gaps:** No other denominations' records were returned by `volume_search` or `collections_search` for this place/period. A separate synthetic/test collection, "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985, listed personCount 982,415) was returned by `collections_search`, but given its labeling as a test fixture it is reported here for completeness rather than relied upon as a genuine collection.
- **Language:** English and German (Lutheran volume).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850 and 1860 U.S. Federal Census coverage confirmed for Schuylkill County via `volume_search` (image group 007621224, 1850–1860, 412 images, 96% name-indexed, full-text searchable) — **indexed + images**. Also externally linked: Ancestry's "1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/).
- **State/provincial census:** Not confirmed by tool output.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850–1885) were mentioned only in the generic "Genealogy Records" wiki page as a general U.S. record type, not confirmed specifically for Schuylkill County by any place-specific tool result in this survey.
- **Access:** 1850/1860 federal census: indexed and image-viewable per `volume_search` above.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, inventories, administrations (general categories per the generic wiki pages); not itemized specifically for Schuylkill County by any tool result.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not applicable — no specific individual named in this survey.
- **Date range:** `volume_search` returned a Probate Records volume for Schuylkill County dated 1845–1880 (image group 004812990, 286 images, 4% name-indexed, full-text searchable) — classify as **full-text searchable, not name-indexed** (flagged explicitly; do not treat as fully indexed). `collections_search` also returned "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (id 1999196, personCount 0), a statewide collection with no person count returned.
- **Where held:** Digitized by FamilySearch per the above; no physical repository confirmed by tool output.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Not confirmed by tool output.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed; no `{Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property` page was fetched in this survey.
- **Types:** Not confirmed for this place.
- **Date range:** Not confirmed.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The 1840s–1860s period spans the Mexican-American War (1846–1848) and the Civil War (1861–1865), but no Schuylkill-County-specific military record was returned by any tool in this survey.
- **Record types / where held:** Not confirmed by tool output for this place.

### Cemetery records
Not confirmed by tool output in this survey — no cemetery-specific collection, volume, or external link was returned for Schuylkill County.

### Newspaper records
Not confirmed by tool output in this survey.

### Immigration/emigration records
Given the German-language Lutheran church volume noted above, immigration-related records (declarations of intention, naturalizations) are plausible, but none were returned by `catalog_search` (0 hits) or `volume_search` for this place and period.

### Tax records
`external_links_search` returned "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) — this predates the 1840s–1860s target window and is listed as background/adjacent coverage only, not as a source for this period.

### Other record types
None confirmed by tool output.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1850–1860 Federal Census (image group 007621224); Probate Records 1845–1880 (image group 004812990); Lutheran Church Records 1840–1875 (image group 004288771); "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196) | Census coverage; probate coverage (full-text, not indexed); pre-civil-registration vital events (Lutheran church, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | "1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/); "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) | 1850 census coverage; pre-period tax-list background | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned `totalResults: 3` with `complete: true` — all matching digitized volumes for this place/period were detailed above, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
Not confirmed by tool output — `catalog_search` returned `totalHits: 0` for this place, a cataloguing gap, not evidence that no physical holdings exist. No courthouse, state archive, or historical-society holding could be named from tool results in this survey.

## Records NOT online
No vital records (births/marriages/deaths) register, land records, military records, cemetery records, or newspaper holdings were returned online for Schuylkill County in this survey — their existence and location are unconfirmed, not ruled out.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey stated that any Schuylkill County record series was destroyed or lost. This should not be read as confirmation that none were.

## Research tips
- The generic FamilySearch Wiki pages returned in this survey ("Genealogy Research Guide," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide, and "Genealogy Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) note that "many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s" and that church records "often predate civil registration by decades or centuries" — apply this generally, but it is not Schuylkill-County- or Pennsylvania-specific guidance.
- The Lutheran church register (image group 004288771) is partly in German and is entirely browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) — budget time to browse image by image and to read German-language entries.
- The probate volume (image group 004812990) is full-text searchable but only 4% name-indexed — use full-text search rather than relying on a name index.
- Use the 1850 and 1860 federal census (96% indexed, full-text searchable) as a first-pass tool to locate the family and household before turning to the harder-to-search probate and church sources.
- `catalog_search` returned zero hits for Schuylkill County — this is a cataloguing gap in the data available to this survey, not proof that no microfilm, manuscript, or finding-aid holdings exist; a direct search of the FamilySearch Catalog website is recommended.
- `place_population` returned no data for this place — population figures for context should be sought elsewhere if needed.

---
Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, in the 1840s through 1860s has solid online census coverage for 1850 and 1860, held free at FamilySearch and also on Ancestry, which is a good starting point for finding a family. Beyond that, the only other materials this search turned up were a probate-records collection that can be searched by typed text but not by an indexed name list, and a Lutheran church register (partly in German) that has no index at all and must be paged through image by image; no vital-records (birth/marriage/death), land, military, cemetery, or newspaper holdings for the county turned up online in this search, which means those records may still exist only on paper at a courthouse, state archive, or church archive that this search could not identify, and a planned visit or written request may be needed. Next, the unconfirmed areas — the county's exact founding history, land and military records, and physical repository holdings — would benefit from a follow-up search of the FamilySearch Catalog directly and a look at Pennsylvania's specific vital-records wiki page, which this survey was unable to retrieve.

# Locality Guide: Mississippi Territory (present-day Alabama) — c. 1800

## Jurisdiction Overview
Alabama did not exist as a jurisdiction until statehood in **1819**. For an ancestor living around 1800 in that region, the controlling jurisdiction was the **Mississippi Territory**, organized in 1798 from land ceded by Georgia and Spanish West Florida. Its government sat at Natchez, and the first county in what is now Alabama — **Washington County** — was formed in 1800, with Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), and Mobile (1812) following. The territory split in 1817 into the State of Mississippi and the **Alabama Territory**, which became the State of Alabama in 1819.

> **Key search tip:** Because Alabama's standardized place record begins only in 1819, all pre-statehood research must be conducted under "Mississippi Territory" in catalogs and databases — searching "Alabama" alone will miss territorial-era material.

---

## Archives & Repositories

### Online Repositories (confirmed by tools this session)

| Repository | Collections | Period Covered | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907" (312,450 people) | Directly covers your period | Free |
| **FamilySearch** | "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920" (245,670 people) | Probate, court records | Free |
| **FamilySearch** | "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890" (198,340 people) | Territorial censuses | Free |
| **FamilySearch** | "Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950" (87,654 people) | Church registers | Free |
| **FamilySearch (browse-only)** | "Territorial land and court records, 1799–1817" — image group 004498712, 143 images, **0% indexed** | Land & court | Must be browsed image by image; free |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal land entry files, **Record Group 49** | Federal land sales from 1803 | Free; in-person or mail request |
| **BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov)** | St. Stephens and Huntsville land office patents from 1803 | Early land grants | Free online |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **Mississippi Department of Archives and History** (Jackson, MS) | Territorial census enumerations: 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, 1816 | In-person / mail request |
| **Alabama Department of Archives and History** (Montgomery, AL) | Territorial census enumerations for the Alabama portion | In-person / mail request |
| **County courthouse** (Washington, Madison, Baldwin, or Mobile Co.) | Probate, court, and deed records; depends on your ancestor's exact location | In-person / mail |

---

## Record Types for This Period

### Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
No civil vital-registration system is documented for the Mississippi Territory at this period — no start date was confirmed by tools this session. **Church records, probate files, and land records serve as the primary substitutes for vital records.**

### Census / Population Lists
Territorial census enumerations in **1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816** are held at the Mississippi and Alabama state archives. FamilySearch's compiled census substitutes collection (1792–1890) also covers the window.

### Land Records
Federal land sales through the **St. Stephens and Huntsville land offices** began in 1803 and are among the strongest sources for identifying early Alabama settlers. Check both NARA (RG 49) and the BLM GLO website. FamilySearch's territorial land records collection (1798–1907) is the main online source.

### Church Records
FamilySearch holds a church records collection beginning in 1800. No specific denominations or surviving register dates before 1800 were confirmed in this survey.

### Court & Probate Records
FamilySearch's county court records collection (1799–1920) covers this period. Check both wills (testate) and administration records once you identify the specific county.

### Tax Records
No territorial tax-list collection was found in this survey — a documented gap, not proof the records don't exist. Consult the Mississippi and Alabama state archives directly.

### Military Records
No conflict-specific collections for the territorial period were returned. Pre-statehood militia records, if they survive, would be at NARA or the state archives.

---

## Known Record Losses
No tool result in this survey reported that specific record series were destroyed. This is not confirmation of survival — the fate of some records was simply not addressed by the sources consulted.

---

## Recommended First Steps

1. **Pin down the exact location.** Where within present-day Alabama did your ancestor live? That determines which of the early counties (Washington, Madison, Baldwin, or Mobile) held authority over their records.
2. **Search the territorial land records.** Federal land sales (from 1803) and the FamilySearch territorial land collection are the most reliably indexed sources for this era.
3. **Check the territorial censuses.** Contact the Mississippi and Alabama state archives to request the 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816 enumerations for the Alabama portion of the territory.
4. **Browse the unindexed FamilySearch volume.** Image group 004498712 (143 images, 1799–1817) must be read page by page but covers land and court records for the territorial period.
5. **Contact the archives directly.** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for this specific jurisdiction could not be retrieved during this survey, so some record-availability details remain unconfirmed — an archivist at MDAH or ADAH will know what survives.

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Post / Arkansas Region (pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Period, 1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Period covered:** 1763–1800 (Spanish Louisiana period); France had established Arkansas Post in 1686, Spain took sovereignty via the 1763 Treaty of Paris, and Spain secretly retroceded the territory to France in 1800 — just before the 1803 Louisiana Purchase.
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post, the colonial civil and military post for the entire region, administered from New Orleans as part of Spanish Louisiana.
- **Religious presence:** Roman Catholic only — the sole organized denomination at the post during this period.
- **Population:** Primarily French and Spanish colonists, enslaved and free people of African descent, and Quapaw Native Americans.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(primary vital-record substitute)*
- **Types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials in sacramental registers; also civil/military censuses (*padrones*) kept alongside them.
- **Language:** Spanish (some pre-1763 entries in French).
- **Online:** One digitized FamilySearch volume exists — image group **008814402**, Spanish-language sacramental register, **1763–1800**, 64 images, **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — browse only, page by page. This is the only confirmed online source for this period.
- **Physical repositories:** Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) · Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock · Library of Congress (microfilm) · Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain).

### Census / Population Enumerations
- U.S. federal census (began 1790) **did not cover** Spanish Arkansas.
- **Spanish colonial *padrones*** (administrative enumerations) were kept at Arkansas Post alongside sacramental registers — these are the census substitute for the period.
- Access: browse-only at best; no indexed collection was found for 1763–1800.

### Land Records
- Spanish-era land **concessions** (not U.S. rectangular-survey patents) were granted under Spanish authority.
- No specific grant index or volume was confirmed online; likely held at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias.

### Military Records
- Arkansas Post was a Spanish military garrison; garrison rosters and post records are referenced generally.
- Likely held at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville) for Spanish military administrative records — not independently confirmed online.

### Civil Vital Registration
- **Did not exist** under Spanish colonial administration; church sacramental records are the only vital-record substitute.

### Probate, Court, Tax, Cemetery, Newspaper Records
- No collection or repository for these record types in this period was returned by any tool query. Treat as a **confirmed coverage gap** — contact the Arkansas History Commission directly.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | 1 digitized volume (image group 008814402): Spanish-language sacramental registers, Arkansas Post, 1763–1800, 64 images | Free; browse-only, no name search |
| **FamilySearch Wiki** | "Arkansas Genealogy" article — Colonial Records / Church Records sections name the key repositories | Free |

### Physical / By Request
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) | Transcriptions of Spanish colonial sacramental registers and colonial records |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Original Spanish colonial administrative, military, and land records for Spanish Louisiana |
| **Library of Congress** (Washington, DC) | Microfilm of surviving Spanish colonial records |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original or earliest surviving sacramental registers from Arkansas Post |

---

## Records NOT Online
Spanish colonial land concessions, military garrison records, and administrative records for this period were **not found in any indexed or searchable online form**. The one FamilySearch church-register volume is browse-only. Any material beyond that must be sought in person or by written request at the physical repositories above.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Use "Arkansas Post" as your place name**, not a modern county — FamilySearch's own volume tags this material to "Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, Arkansas, United States" even though no county government existed yet. Searching by modern county names will miss it.

2. **Plan to read Spanish** — the one digitized volume is in Spanish, with possible French-language entries from the pre-1763 era. If you can't read it yourself, a translator will be needed.

3. **Browse the volume page by page** — image group 008814402 on FamilySearch, 64 images, no name index. There is no shortcut; every page must be read.

4. **Contact the Arkansas History Commission first** for researchers who cannot travel to Spain — they hold transcriptions of the Spanish colonial material and can advise on what survives.

5. **Check both Spanish and French administrative naming** — because Spain retroceded Louisiana to France in 1800 before the 1803 Purchase, records near the end of this period could appear under either convention.

6. **Bridge forward with later records** — the FamilySearch collection "Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870" (178,345 people) can help you trace the same families into the territorial and statehood period once an Arkansas Post connection is suspected.

---

**Bottom line:** Almost no modern-style government records exist for pre-1800 Arkansas — the Catholic mission at Arkansas Post was the only record-keeper. Its one surviving Spanish-language register (1763–1800) is viewable online but only page by page. Beyond that, land grants, military rosters, and fuller church registers survive only on paper at a handful of archives in Little Rock, Washington DC, and Seville. The recommended first step is a written request to the **Arkansas History Commission** and the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** to determine exactly what they hold.

- **Formed:** Arkansas Post was established by the French in 1686 as the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley; sovereignty passed to Spain after the 1763 Treaty of Paris, and Spain secretly retroceded the territory to France in 1800, shortly before the 1803 Louisiana Purchase brought it under American control (Wikipedia: Arkansas).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Arkansas Post served as the colonial civil and military post for the region; modern "Arkansas, United States" as a standardized FamilySearch place only dates from statehood in 1836, so no FamilySearch place record exists yet for the 1763–1800 Spanish period itself.

- **Economy:** Fur trade, frontier agriculture, and military garrison activity centered on Arkansas Post.
- **Ethnic composition:** French and Spanish colonists, enslaved and free people of African descent, and Native American (notably Quapaw) populations in and around the post, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result on "Arkansas Genealogy."
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (French/Spanish colonial mission), the only organized church presence at the post during this period.
- **Key historical events:** Transfer from French to Spanish control (1763), secret retrocession to France (1800), and the subsequent Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary changes
- Arkansas Post itself predates any county structure; the territory was governed directly as part of Spanish Louisiana, not as a distinct jurisdiction with its own civil records office.
- Records from this period are filed under "Arkansas Post" as a place name, not under the modern state or county system — `volume_search` returns this material tagged to "Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, Arkansas, United States" even though no county government existed at the time, so search by that place string rather than a modern county name.
- No FamilySearch standardPlace exists for the colonial-era jurisdiction itself (the tool's earliest standardized "Arkansas" record dates only from 1836); treat this as a confirmed gap in the place database for this period, not a sign the records don't exist.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No FamilySearch Wiki page returned jurisdiction-specific registration dates for this period — the `Arkansas_Vital_Records` URL redirected to a generic "Genealogy Records" page with no Arkansas-specific content, and civil (non-church) vital registration did not exist under Spanish colonial administration regardless.

- **Where held:** Not applicable as a separate civil series for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Sacramental (church) registers are the vital-record substitute for this entire period.

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, the sole organized denomination at Arkansas Post in this period.

### Census records

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Ohio, United States (ca. 1788–1803, Pre-Statehood Northwest Territory)

## Jurisdiction Overview

In 1790, Ohio was **not yet a state** — it was part of the Northwest Territory, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio became the first state carved from that territory in **1803**. The administrative center was **Washington County** (organized 1788), the first county in the territory; **Hamilton County** followed in 1790.

---

## Boundary Changes

Boundary changes in this era were **frequent and significant**. Washington County (1788) originally covered a vast area; Hamilton County was organized in 1790 from the remainder. Any ancestor in "Ohio" in 1790 was legally in one of these two enormous counties (or unorganized territory). Their boundaries were repeatedly redrawn as new counties were carved out through statehood and beyond — so researchers must determine **which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event**, not assume today's county lines apply.

> Per the FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes section: "Boundary changes were frequent — researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event."

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- No statewide birth/death registration existed in 1790.
- **Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013** (FamilySearch collection 1803785, ~3M people) begins right at the edge of this period — pre-1803 county marriage records *may* exist for Washington/Hamilton counties.
- **Ohio, County Death Records** (collection 1417891) only starts in **1840** — a confirmed gap for 1790.
- **Alternatives:** Church records and county marriage registers.

### Church Records
- **Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950** (FamilySearch collection 2246917, ~678K people) covers 1790 directly. This is a primary substitute for missing civil vital registration.

### Census Records
- The **1790 federal census did not cover the Northwest Territory** — it was not yet organized as a state or listed territory in that enumeration. The 1790–1800 period is effectively a **federal census gap** for this area.
- **Alternative:** Use tax lists in place of census records.

### Land Records
Two overlapping, historically distinct land-grant systems operated here:
- **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans, surveyed by metes and bounds. Warrants held at the **Virginia State Library**.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): surveyed on a rectangular grid. Records held at the **Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland**.
- **FamilySearch:** "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (collection 1542187, ~234K people) covers 1790.
- A browse-only volume of **Territorial Land Records, Northwest Territory, 1788–1799** (image group 005112233, 51 images, 0% indexed) exists — must be browsed image by image.

### Tax Records
- **Washington County, Ohio tax volume, 1799–1803** (image group 005112240, 73 images, 12% name-indexed) — a key substitute for the missing 1790–1800 federal census.
- **Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850** (FamilySearch collection 1987542, ~345K people) begins just after the target period.

### Military Records
- Bounty-land warrant records tied to Revolutionary War service are likely relevant (given the Virginia Military District), but no specific collection was confirmed in this search. Try the **National Archives (NARA)** for service, pension, and bounty-land records.

### Probate and Court Records
- Early Washington and Hamilton County court records are the expected custodians, but no online collection was found in this survey — treat these as **physical-repository-only** until confirmed otherwise.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church records (1787+), county marriages (1789+), land records (1787+), tax records (1800+) | Free |
| Virginia State Library | Virginia Military District land warrants | In-person / mail |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person / mail |
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Early territorial court and land records | In-person / request |
| County courthouses (Washington, Hamilton) | Deeds, probate, court minute books | In-person / mail |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal land, military, court records | Free (originals by request) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Determine county jurisdiction first.** Pin down whether your ancestor's location fell under Washington County or Hamilton County before searching county-level records — the boundary lines shifted repeatedly.

2. **Identify the land-grant district** (Virginia Military District vs. Connecticut Western Reserve vs. general federal public land) before choosing a land-records repository — each has a different custodian and survey system.

3. **Use tax lists as a census substitute.** The 1790–1800 federal census gap for this area makes early tax lists (especially the Washington County volume, 1799–1803) an essential alternative.

4. **Church records are your primary vital record source.** Civil registration did not exist. The FamilySearch "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" collection (2246917) covers this period directly.

5. **Some early volumes are browse-only** (0% indexed). The territorial land records volume (1788–1799) must be paged through image by image.

6. **Consult the live FamilySearch Wiki directly** for Ohio-specific pages on vital records, land records, census, and church records — several specific Ohio Wiki pages returned only generic content in this search and could not be confirmed with detail here.

---

**Bottom line:** Ohio in 1790 was raw frontier territory under the Northwest Ordinance, with just two enormous and frequently-redrawn counties. There was no census coverage and no civil vital registration, but church registers (1787+), county marriage records (1789+), land records tied to two special grant systems, and early tax lists fill most of the gap. The most critical first step is pinpointing which county — Washington or Hamilton — governed the specific location, and which land-grant district it fell within, before choosing where to search.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Statehood:** California became a U.S. state in **1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely.
- **Key hubs:** San Francisco and Sacramento were the principal boomtowns.
- **Context:** Roughly 300,000 migrants arrived between 1848–1855, drawn by gold discovered at Sutter's Mill on January 24, 1848. The population was transient, predominantly male, and highly diverse in origin.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **California, County Births, 1850–1919** — FamilySearch collection 2017276 (~789,000 persons), held at the county level.
- **California, County Marriages, 1850–1952** — FamilySearch collection 1452832 (~1.1 million persons), county level.
- **Pre-statehood alternative:** Franciscan mission registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) covered 1769–1850 → **California, Mission Records, 1769–1850** (FamilySearch collection 1804372, ~99,000 persons; records generally in Spanish).

### Census Records
- **1850 Federal Census** — the first taken in California, but some county returns are **missing or partially destroyed**; essential but incomplete.
- **California State Census, 1850–1852** — FamilySearch image group 006601001 (88% name-indexed, full-text searchable); a valuable substitute where the federal census has gaps.

### Mining & Land Records
- **Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco, 1849–1855** — FamilySearch image group 006601002 (340 images, **0% indexed, browse-only**). Must be examined page by page; no name search available.
- General land patents in federal land states route through the **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov), though California-specific detail was not confirmed by this survey's tools.

### Immigration / Passenger Records
- **Ship passenger manifests, San Francisco** — held at **NARA, San Bruno** (National Archives, San Francisco Bay Area). Examine the full manifest, not just name indexes, as children frequently appear unindexed.
- **Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858** — FamilySearch image group 006601003 (298 images, **0% indexed, browse-only**).

### Later Settlement Records (Post–Gold Rush)
- **California, Great Registers, 1866–1910** — FamilySearch collection 1923340 (~1.3 million persons; voter registration). Begins in 1866 — documents those who *stayed*, not the initial 1848–1855 wave; useful for tracking a miner's settled years.

### Church Records
- Franciscan Catholic mission records are the primary pre-1850 vital-event source (see Mission Records collection above).
- No Gold Rush–era Protestant or other denominational collections were returned by this survey's tools — treat as a coverage gap, not confirmed absence.

### Other Record Types (Not Confirmed Online)
- Probate, court, and tax records are held at the county courthouse level; no specific California collection was confirmed by tools in this survey.
- Cemetery, newspaper, and military record collections specific to this era were not returned by tools; use the external repositories listed below as starting points.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | County births/marriages 1850+; Mission Records; State Census 1850–52; Mining Claim Registers; Port Arrival Registers; Great Registers 1866+ | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census collection (supplements the partially destroyed 1850 CA census) | Subscription |
| **NARA Online (Fold3 / Archives.gov)** | Military records; San Francisco passenger manifests | Free / Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical California newspapers | Subscription |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives, San Bruno (NARA Pacific Region)** | Ship passenger manifests, San Francisco arrivals | In-person / mail |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Gold Rush–era manuscripts, overland trail diaries, journals | In-person |
| **California State Library** | Gold Rush–era manuscript collections | In-person |
| **County Courthouses** | Probate, land, mining claim originals | In-person / mail |

---

## Known Record Losses
Some 1850 federal census county returns for California are reported as missing or partially destroyed. The **California State Census, 1850–1852** (FamilySearch image group 006601001) is the most practical substitute — it is 88% indexed and full-text searchable.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1850-52 state census** as a supplement whenever the federal census shows gaps for a particular California county.
2. **Mining Claim Registers and Port Arrival Registers on FamilySearch are browse-only** (0% indexed) — budget time for image-by-image review; there is no name search shortcut.
3. **San Francisco passenger manifests at NARA San Bruno** are critical for documenting a migrant's arrival by sea — examine the full page, not just the index.
4. **Mission Records** (1769–1850) are for families already in California before the Gold Rush, not for the migrants themselves, but they document any California-born women a miner may have married.
5. **Great Registers** (1866+) can confirm that a miner stayed and settled after the rush, and may record birthplace, nativity, and physical description — excellent for linking to earlier records.
6. **Bancroft Library and California State Library** hold unique unpublished materials (diaries, letters, overland journals) not digitized online — worth contacting directly for a forty-niner ancestor.
7. The FamilySearch catalog returned zero hits for California in this survey, which is a cataloguing gap — check the FamilySearch Catalog directly for microfilm holdings not yet surfaced here.

---

This guide covers what the survey's tools confirmed. For a specific county (e.g., El Dorado, Calaveras, Tuolumne — the heart of the Mother Lode), a county-level locality guide would add boundary history and more precise record-set details. A research-plan agent can then turn these record types into a sequenced search plan for a named ancestor.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, California Gold Rush)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state in 1850, bypassing territorial status (per Wikipedia summary of the California Gold Rush).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Varies by county; San Francisco and Sacramento were the chief boomtowns of the era.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (statehood 1850).
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for California, United States for 1848–1860 — this survey could not confirm population figures from that tool.
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated 1848–1855, driving a massive, transient, predominantly male migration (Wikipedia, "California Gold Rush").
- **Ethnic composition:** Migrants came from diverse origins across the U.S. and abroad (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Franciscan mission-era Catholic records predate statehood; later Gold Rush-era denominations are not detailed in the sources retrieved.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; roughly 300,000 migrants arrived; statehood in 1850 (Wikipedia).

## Boundary changes
This survey did not confirm county-level boundary changes within 1848–1860; California's counties were newly organized at statehood. A researcher narrowing to a specific county should request a county-level locality guide for boundary history.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page fetched at the constructed California Vital Records URL redirected to a generic "Genealogy Records" article with no California-specific start date; this survey could not confirm the level (state/county) or year statewide civil registration began in California. The wiki search result names a **California, County Births, 1850-1919** collection (FamilySearch collection 2017276, 789,456 persons) and **California, County Marriages, 1850-1952** (collection 1452832, 1,135,780 persons), both beginning in 1850 and held at the county level.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Franciscan mission registers (1769–1834) recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials before statehood (wiki_search result, "California Genealogy" page, Pre-Statehood Records section: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). FamilySearch's **California, Mission Records, 1769-1850** collection (id 1804372, 98,765 persons) covers this.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Franciscan Catholic missions (pre-1850); other denominations not confirmed by tools in this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (mission records).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "California, Mission Records, 1769-1850" (id 1804372).
- **Gaps:** No Gold Rush-era (1849–1860) Protestant or other denominational collections were returned by `collections_search` — report as a coverage gap, not absence.
- **Language:** Mission records are generally in Spanish; this was not independently confirmed by a tool result here and should be verified before research.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1850 federal census was the first taken in California and is essential for Gold Rush research, but some county returns were partially destroyed (wiki_search, "California Genealogy," Pre-Statehood Records section).
- **State census:** A California State Census volume (image group 006601001) covering 1850–1852 is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable (`volume_search`).

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York — Colonial Period (1700s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Origin:** New York City began as the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam (1624), seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York.
- **Governing jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colonial administration through 1783); New York State was not formed until 1788.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian churches kept extensive records in this period.
- **Key historical events:** Dutch-to-British transfer of control in 1664; NYC served as the provincial capital throughout the colonial era.

---

## Boundary Notes
- Dutch (New Amsterdam, to 1664) and British (New York, 1664–1783) records form one continuous trail and should be searched together.
- New York State as a jurisdiction post-dates the colonial period (formed 1788), so governance and courts were at the provincial level during the 1700s.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(primary substitute for vital registration)*
- **Why central:** No civil birth/marriage/death registration existed in the 1700s. Church registers served that function.
- **Denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest, beginning 1639), Anglican (Trinity Church), Presbyterian.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940" (collection id 1469062, ~2.3 million persons) — covers all denominations at the state scope.
- **Digitized Dutch Reformed volume found:** Image group **007733180**, 211 images, 1700–1776, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in the Dutch language** — browse-only, image by image.
- ⚠️ **Language note:** Dutch Reformed registers from this era are written in Dutch; translation/paleography assistance is needed to read them.

### Probate Records *(wills & estates)*
- **What exists:** Wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York; estate inventories and guardianship files.
- **Published abstracts:** The *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the New-York Historical Society indexes colonial-era wills.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971" (id 1542780, ~987,000 persons) — fully within the 1700s window.

### Land Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975" (id 2078654, ~1.5 million persons) — covers the full colonial period.
- Colonial land patents/conveyances are part of this series.

### Tax Records *(census substitute)*
- **Why important:** No census existed before 1790, so tax assessment lists are the principal population substitute for most of the 1700s.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804" (id 1678432) — slightly post-dates the period but useful as a bridge.
- Earlier ward-level tax lists survive for some years; check directly on FamilySearch's website.

### Military / Militia Records
- Province of New York maintained militia rolls listing men of military age.
- **Access:** FamilySearch and Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) hold relevant military records.

### Census Records
- **Not applicable** for most of the 1700s. The first U.S. federal census is 1790 — after the colonial period ends.
- **Substitute:** Tax lists and militia rolls (see above).

---

## Online Repository Guide

| Repository | Relevant Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church Records 1640–1940 (id 1469062); Land Records 1630–1975 (id 2078654); Probate Records 1629–1971 (id 1542780); Tax Rolls 1799–1804 (id 1678432); Dutch Reformed image volume 007733180 (1700–1776, browse-only) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1790+ only — does not reach colonial period) | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Militia and military service records | Subscription |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal-level military and later records | Free |

---

## Physical Repositories
- **New-York Historical Society** — holds the published *Abstracts of Wills* and extensive colonial-era manuscript holdings.
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society** — holds colonial-era collections (exact holdings not confirmed by tools used in this survey).
- ⚠️ No addresses, hours, or access details were returned; contact each institution directly.

---

## Records NOT Online
- The Dutch Reformed Church Registers (1700–1776, image group 007733180) are online but **not searchable** — they must be browsed page by page in Dutch.
- FamilySearch's catalog search returned **zero hits** for New York City at the city and state level — this is a tool-side gap, not evidence the records don't exist. Search the FamilySearch Catalog directly at familysearch.org.
- Anglican (Trinity Church) and Presbyterian registers are named in the FamilySearch Wiki but were not individually returned as browsable volumes in this survey.

---

## Known Record Losses
No tool result confirmed that any specific New York City colonial-era record series was destroyed or lost. This is a gap in what was checked, not a confirmation of survival.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with church records** — the Dutch Reformed, Trinity (Anglican), and Presbyterian registers are the main substitute for absent civil registration. FamilySearch collection id 1469062 covers all three.
2. **Browse the Dutch Reformed volume** (image group 007733180) page by page — it is 0%-indexed and in Dutch; plan time for reading Dutch handwriting, or use a translation agent.
3. **Search probate records early** — wills often name children, grandchildren, and in-laws, making them one of the richest sources for colonial family reconstruction. Start with the *Abstracts of Wills* series (New-York Historical Society) and FamilySearch collection id 1542780.
4. **Use tax lists as a census substitute** — militia rolls and tax assessment lists can establish residence and place a man in a specific ward before 1790.
5. **Vital records start date is unconfirmed** — FamilySearch Wiki returned a generic, non-jurisdiction-specific page for New York vital records; check the wiki directly at familysearch.org for the actual start of civil registration.
6. **Search FamilySearch Catalog directly** — the catalog tool returned 0 hits for this area; this appears to be a tool-side limitation. Many colonial-era microfilm reels are likely listed on the FamilySearch website catalog.

---

If you'd like to go further, share an ancestor's name, approximate birth/death dates, and religion (if known), and I can search within the Dutch Reformed church collection and the probate/land records identified above, or build a step-by-step research plan.

## Jurisdiction overview

- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City itself was the provincial capital of the Province of New York through much of the colonial era.

- **Economy:** Major commercial port and administrative center under British rule (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian churches kept extensive records (Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki search result, "New York City Genealogy" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Key historical events:** Dutch-to-British transfer of control in 1664; the city served briefly as the first U.S. capital after the colonial period ended (Wikipedia).

## Boundary changes
- The colony transitioned from Dutch (New Amsterdam, to 1664) to British administration (New York, 1664–1783); records from the Dutch period and early British period form one continuous trail and should be searched together rather than as separate record sets.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- Virginia became a state in 1776 upon declaring independence; prior to that it was a colony.
- Richmond served as the state's seat of government during the war.
- Virginia contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony, and major battles — including Yorktown — were fought on Virginia soil.
- **Important loss:** Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed in the 1814 burning of Washington, D.C. records. County tax lists from the 1780s are the standard substitute.

---

## Military Records — The Core Source Type

| Record Type | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Continental Line service records & muster rolls (RG 93) | National Archives (NARA) | archives.gov |
| Pension & bounty-land warrant application files (RG 15) | National Archives (NARA) | archives.gov |
| Virginia militia records | Library of Virginia, Richmond | In-person / by request |
| Virginia State Navy records | Virginia State Library | In-person / mail |
| **FamilySearch:** Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (id 1945678, ~345,678 people, indexed) | FamilySearch.org | Free |

> **Tip:** Pension and bounty-land warrant files (NARA RG 15) often contain the richest genealogical detail — ages, residences, and family members — and are worth checking even when a muster-roll entry has already been found.

---

## Land Records — Bounty Warrants for Veterans

- Virginia granted land bounty warrants to Revolutionary War veterans, with warrant and survey records held at the **Virginia State Library**.
- A digitized browse-only volume of Virginia bounty warrants, 1779–1800 (FamilySearch image group 005301447, 341 images), is available online but is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image.
- The broader **FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900"** (id 1734285, ~2.5 million people) is indexed and covers the war years.

---

## Tax Records — Substitute for the Missing Census

Because the 1790 census was destroyed, **county personal property and land tax lists from the 1780s** are the primary substitute for locating families around that time:
- **FamilySearch:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (id 1456723, indexed)
- **Browse-only digitized volume:** State enumerations / tax lists, 1782–1799 (image group 005301449, full-text searchable, not name-indexed)

---

## Court & Probate Records

- **FamilySearch:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (id 2134567, ~1.7 million people)
- **FamilySearch:** "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (id 1734285)
- A specific browse-only volume of **Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795** (image group 005301448, 158 images) is only 61% name-searchable — most pages must be browsed by image.

---

## Church Records

- **FamilySearch:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (id 1598230, ~1.2 million people) overlaps the entire war period.
- No civil vital registration existed in Virginia during this era; church registers are the primary substitute for births and deaths.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Role | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Indexed military, land, church, court, and tax records for Virginia | Free |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | Federal military service records and pension files | Free / by request |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records aggregator | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Wartime notices, casualty reports | Subscription |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records |
| Virginia State Library | Bounty-land warrant and survey records |
| County courthouses | Original court order books, deeds, wills |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Search tax lists first** (1782–1850 on FamilySearch) as a stand-in for the destroyed 1790 census.
2. **Check both NARA record groups** — Continental Line service records (RG 93) and pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) are separate record systems.
3. **Request militia records** from the Library of Virginia directly, as militia service was a state-level (not federal) system.
4. **Browse unindexed volumes by image** for Augusta County court orders and the Revolutionary War land bounty warrants — name searches will not find entries in those volumes.
5. If you have a **specific county**, a county-level guide can identify the parent-county record trail and any local boundary changes.

---

If you have a specific ancestor's name, county, or type of service in mind, I can build a focused research plan or search the military and land record collections directly.

- **Ethnic composition:** Not confirmed by tool results for this survey.

- **Key historical events:** Virginia contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony, and major Revolutionary War battles, including Yorktown, were fought on Virginia soil (Wikipedia, "Virginia").

## Boundary changes
Virginia's county boundaries shifted repeatedly in the 18th century as new counties were formed from older ones, but no county-specific boundary change for the 1775–1783 period was surfaced by this survey (which was run at the state level, per the delegation's scope). Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed — per the FamilySearch Wiki chunk on "Virginia Military Records," it was burned along with other Washington, D.C. records in 1814. ## Research tips
- Search county tax lists from the 1780s as a substitute for the destroyed 1790 census, per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Virginia Military Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- Check both Continental Line service records (NARA RG 93) and Virginia militia records (Library of Virginia), since the two systems were recorded separately, per the same page.
- Pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA RG 15) often contain the richest genealogical detail — ages, residences, family members — and should be checked even when a soldier's muster-roll entry has already been found.
- Browse the Augusta County court order books (1775–1795) and the Revolutionary War land bounty warrant volume directly by image, since both are largely or entirely unindexed.
- The constructed FamilySearch Wiki pages for "Virginia_Vital_Records" and "Virginia_Land_and_Property" did not return Virginia-specific content in this survey — re-check those pages directly before concluding no registration or land-office detail exists for this period.

I looked into Virginia for the Revolutionary War years, 1775 to 1783. The strongest wartime sources are military and pension files kept by the National Archives, militia records at the Library of Virginia, and bounty-land warrants connecting veterans to land claims at the Virginia State Library, plus digitized FamilySearch collections covering Virginia military records, land and wills, and county court records for this era. Two things to keep in mind: the 1790 census was destroyed in an 1814 fire, so 1780s county tax lists are the standard stand-in for finding a family around that time, and several of the key digitized volumes (the Augusta County court order books and the land bounty warrants) are not name-searchable and have to be browsed page by page rather than searched by name.

Next, if you have a specific county or ancestor's name in mind, I can build a focused research plan or search the relevant military and land record collections directly.

The locality guide has been saved as **loc_001** for New Orleans, Louisiana (1800–1830). Here is what it found:

---

## New Orleans Early 1800s — Record Survival & Substitutes

### Disasters That Damaged Records
- **Two major fires** (1788 and 1794) destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records.
- **Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods** caused further archival damage in later years.

### What Survived & Where to Look

#### 1. St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers
- **What they are:** Catholic baptism, marriage, and burial records.
- **Coverage:** Back to 1731, though with gaps.
- **Why they matter:** In a heavily Catholic city, these church records often substitute for missing civil vital records.

#### 2. New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center
- **What they are:** Notarial acts — legal and property documents.
- **Coverage:** Over 30 million pages dating back to 1734.
- **Why they matter:** Louisiana's French-derived **civil-law system** used notaries for many transactions (property sales, successions, contracts, wills) that other states would record elsewhere. These are essential substitutes for missing deeds, wills, and probate records.

#### 3. FamilySearch — Notarial Microfilm Images (1803–1820)
- A digitized but **unindexed** set of notarial microfilm images was located on FamilySearch.
- These can only be **browsed page by page** (not searched by name).
- Many records are **in French**, so translation may be needed.

---

### Important Caveats
- Some FamilySearch Wiki pages for this locality could not be retrieved, so a few specifics (such as the exact start date of Louisiana civil birth/death registration) remain **unconfirmed** from this survey rather than assumed.
- Sources and collections named above were returned by the guide's own tool searches — not from general knowledge.

---

**Suggested next step:** A research plan can now be built to decide which of these record sets — the cathedral registers, the notarial archive, or the FamilySearch collections — to search first for your specific ancestors. Just say the word!

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Louisiana (1800-1830)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Founded by the French in 1718; passed to Spain in 1763, briefly back to France, then to the United States via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803; Louisiana became a state in 1812.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans is itself the seat of Orleans Parish.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana, United States.
- **Economy:** Port and trade city; civil-law legal tradition (Napoleonic Code) rather than English common law, which shapes record types (notarial acts, successions, tutorships, interdictions rather than deeds/wills in the common-law sense).
- **Ethnic composition:** French and Spanish colonial populations, free people of color, enslaved people, and growing Anglo-American population after 1803 (per Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral) was dominant through this period.
- **Key historical events:** Fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records; the Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred the territory to the US; repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes and floods further damaged archival holdings (per Wikipedia and FamilySearch Wiki).

## Boundary changes
- Louisiana Territory became the State of Louisiana in 1812; New Orleans and Orleans Parish boundaries were not reported as changing within 1800-1830 by the tools consulted.
- Records from the colonial (French/Spanish) period before 1803 were created under those governments and are held separately from later US-era civil records (see Notarial Archives, below).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The Louisiana Statewide Death Index collection begins in 1819 (collections_search), but this is a derivative index, not proof statewide civil registration began that year; the Louisiana_Vital_Records wiki page could not be resolved to jurisdiction-specific content in this survey, so the exact registration level and start year are not confirmed here.
- **What exists:** No indexed civil birth/marriage records specific to 1800-1830 were returned; a death index collection (1819-1964) was found.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge, per FamilySearch Wiki search result.
- **Gaps:** Civil vital registration appears limited or absent for this early period; church sacramental registers are the primary substitute (see below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral) dominant in this period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 (with gaps), per FamilySearch Wiki search result (New Orleans Genealogy, 'Records Surviving Disasters').
- **Where held:** Parish/archdiocesan archives; also appears in FamilySearch's "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" collection (id 1612905, 987,654 persons, collections_search).
- **Gaps:** Pre-1794 registers may be incomplete owing to the 1788 and 1794 fires; exact loss extent not stated by any tool result consulted.
- **Language:** French and Spanish for the colonial period; collection volume 004990115 (notarial, 1803-1820) is noted in French and English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Louisiana joined the US in 1812; the earliest federal census covering it as a state is 1820 (1810 Louisiana census exists per national pattern, not independently confirmed by a tool result here).
- **State/provincial census:** Not confirmed by tools consulted.
- **Access:** Not detailed by collections_search or volume_search results for this place/period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Successions (Louisiana's civil-law equivalent of probate), tutorships (guardianship), interdictions.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch's "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" collection (id 2078341, 456,789 persons) covers this period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana courts and the Louisiana State Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system and land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not stated by any tool result in this survey.
- **Types:** Notarial acts record most property transactions in this civil-law jurisdiction rather than county-style deeds.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734, per FamilySearch Wiki search result); a browse-only FamilySearch microfilm volume of notarial acts, 1803-1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, French/English, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable) also exists.

### Military records
- Not detailed by tool results for this place/period; the War of 1812 (including the 1815 Battle of New Orleans) falls in this window and NARA-held service/pension files are the standard national source, per the generic FamilySearch guide consulted.

### Cemetery records
- Not detailed by any tool result for this place/period; no FindAGrave-specific New Orleans data returned.

### Newspaper records
- Not detailed by any tool result in this survey.

### Immigration/emigration records
- New Orleans was a major port of entry in this period; passenger lists and naturalization records would be expected at NARA, but no place-specific collection was returned by the tools consulted.

### Tax records
- Not detailed by any tool result in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 persons); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (1,135,780 persons); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 persons); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (2,345,678 persons) | Substitutes for missing early civil vital and probate records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | General census coverage | Subscription |
| FamilySearch Wiki | Vital Records category page | General reference | Free |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (general site, not place-specific results returned) | Cemetery records gap | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (general site, not place-specific results returned) | Newspaper records gap | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (general site, not place-specific results returned) | Military records gap | Subscription |
| National Archives (NARA) | Federal records generally | Immigration, naturalization, military gaps | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** Only one digitized volume (image group 004990115) matched New Orleans/Orleans Parish for 1800-1820 in volume_search; it is browse-only. The FamilySearch Catalog returned zero hits for this place in this search (a cataloguing gap, not evidence records don't exist).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — 1840s Immigration Focus

## Jurisdiction Overview
Boston is a long-established city within Suffolk County, Massachusetts — one of the principal U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s. This decade saw a massive surge of Irish immigration during the Great Famine (1845–1852); by 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born.

---

## Key Record Types for 1840s Boston Immigrants

### 1. Customs Passenger Lists (Primary Source)
- **Series:** National Archives Record Group 36 — "Passenger Lists, Port of Boston," 1820–1891
- **What they record:** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin (1840s lists are sparse compared to later Ellis Island–era manifests)
- **Digitized volume found:** Image group **003345210**, covering 1840–1850 (389 images) — only **3% name-indexed** but **full-text searchable**; use keyword/text search, not a name index alone
- **Online collections:**
  - **FamilySearch** collection **1784312**, "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (~1.23M people) — free
  - **Ancestry** also holds indexes/images of this series — subscription required
- **Physical originals:** National Archives at Boston (Waltham) — in-person or written request

### 2. Catholic Parish Registers
- **Why essential:** Civil registration is thin for this period; Catholic church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are often the only way to reconstruct families after arrival
- **Key parishes:** Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's, which grew rapidly to serve Irish immigrants
- **Where held:** **Archdiocese of Boston Archives**
- **Online:** FamilySearch collection **1921657**, "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" — free

### 3. Naturalization Records
- For post-arrival naturalization — scattered across federal, state, and local courts
- **FamilySearch collection 1459213**, "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" — free

### 4. Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **FamilySearch collection 2061550**, "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" — overlaps this period

### 5. Federal Census Records
- The **1840** and **1850** U.S. federal censuses both fall within this window and are excellent for locating recently arrived families

### 6. Probate Records
- **FamilySearch collection 1678901**, "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991"

### 7. The Pilot (Newspaper)
- Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper published **arrival notices** and **missing-persons advertisements** — invaluable for Famine-era immigrants. Check Newspapers.com or local archives.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger lists, church records, naturalization, vital records | Free |
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham) | Original RG 36 customs passenger lists | In-person / written request |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives directly |
| Ancestry | Census records, passenger list images | Subscription |

---

## Key Research Tips

- **1840s manifests are thin** — only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin. Don't expect birthplace villages or family relationships on these lists.
- **The Port of Boston 1840–1850 digitized volume (image group 003345210) is only 3% name-indexed** — search it by full-text keyword, not by name index.
- **Catholic parish registers are essential** for reconstructing Irish immigrant families alongside (or before) civil records.
- **The Pilot newspaper** is a uniquely valuable resource for Famine-era Irish immigrants seeking or being sought by relatives.

If you'd like, a research plan can be built from this guide to search specific collections for named ancestors.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts, United States (1840-1850) — Immigration Focus

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Boston is a long-established city (FamilySearch dates its jurisdiction from 1630); Suffolk County, Massachusetts.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** Could not confirm from `place_population` — the tool returned no data for this place/period.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic seaport and one of the principal 1840s U.S. ports of entry.
- **Ethnic composition:** Surge of Irish immigration during the Great Famine (1845-1852); per Wikipedia, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born by 1850.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic parishes (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's) grew rapidly to serve incoming Irish immigrants, per the FamilySearch Wiki.
- **Key historical events:** Irish Famine immigration wave, 1845-1852.

## Boundary changes
Not assessed in detail for this survey — no boundary-change issue was identified as affecting immigration records for this period.

## Available record types

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of Boston — one of the five major U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s (FamilySearch Wiki, "Massachusetts Immigration," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston).
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists, 1820-1891, held in National Archives Record Group 36. Per the same page, 1840s-era lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not the fuller detail of later Ellis-Island-era manifests. A digitized volume matching this place and period was found by `volume_search`: image group 003345210 ("Passenger Lists, Port of Boston," 1840-1850, 389 images), only 3% name-indexed but marked full-text searchable — reachable via full-text search, not reliable for a straight name search.
- **Where held:** Originals at the National Archives at Boston (Waltham), per the FamilySearch Wiki page above. Indexed/digitized versions exist on FamilySearch (collection 1784312, "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891") and on Ancestry, per the same Wiki page.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents — check the full manifest, not just the head of household.
- **Naturalization:** Naturalization records for this period are scattered across federal, state, and local courts, per the generic FamilySearch "Genealogy Records" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records). FamilySearch collection 1459213, "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906," covers this. `catalog_search` for "passenger lists" at this place returned 0 hits — a cataloguing gap, not evidence the records don't exist (they are confirmed above via the Wiki and `volume_search`).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic parishes serving Irish immigrants, including the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's, per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Massachusetts Church Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials from the 1840s onward, per the same page.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Boston archives, per the same page. FamilySearch collection 1921657, "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920," also covers this.

- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection 2061550, "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890," overlaps this period.
- **Where held:** Town-level, per the collection title.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (above).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1840 and 1850 U.S. federal censuses fall within this period; FamilySearch's generic guidance confirms decennial coverage from 1790, but no Boston-specific collection was surfaced by `collections_search` in this result set.
- **Access:** Not detailed by tool results for this specific place beyond the generic statement above.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships — FamilySearch collection 1678901, "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991," covers this period.
- **Where held:** County/district level, per generic FamilySearch guidance; no Suffolk-County-specific repository was returned.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (id 1784312, ~1.23M people); image group 003345210, Port of Boston passenger lists 1840-1850 (full-text searchable, only 3% name-indexed) | Primary immigrant arrival record | Free |
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (id 1921657) | Catholic baptism/marriage/burial records for Irish immigrants | Free |
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906 (id 1459213) | Post-arrival naturalization | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | General census coverage | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| NARA | Holds original RG 36 customs passenger lists | Originals of Port of Boston manifests | In-person/online (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` found exactly one digitized volume matching Boston passenger lists for 1840-1850 (image group 003345210); `totalResults` was 1, so this is the complete matching set for that search, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham) | Original RG 36 customs passenger lists | In-person / written request |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | Contact method not specified by tool results |

## Records NOT online
The original RG 36 customs passenger lists exist only as physical records at NARA-Boston; the online FamilySearch/Ancestry versions are indexes/digitized images of this same series, not independent originals. No tool result confirmed online availability of Suffolk County probate or court records for this period.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey reported any destroyed or lost records for Boston passenger lists or Catholic church records in this period.

## Research tips
- 1840s Boston customs passenger lists record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — much less detail than later manifests, per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Massachusetts Immigration," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston).
