# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (mid-1800s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The region was designated **Indian Territory** under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, used for the forced relocation of tribal nations. It did not become the State of Oklahoma until 1907. No county-level civil jurisdiction existed there in the mid-1800s — authority ran through tribal governments and federal Indian agencies. The Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) relocated via the Trail of Tears and governed themselves under federal oversight.

---

## Boundary Notes

Indian Territory was not organized into counties during this period. Researchers should treat **"Indian Territory"** as the operative jurisdiction — not modern Oklahoma counties — for any mid-1800s research.

---

## Available Record Types

### Tribal Rolls & Enrollment Records
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** and **Drennen Roll (1852)** are the most relevant mid-1800s rolls.
- The later **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** are the most widely used Five Tribes enrollment records (name, age, sex, blood quantum, tribal affiliation) and should be cross-referenced against earlier rolls.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth; Dawes Rolls indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Digitized volume confirmed:** FamilySearch image group **002298871** — "Tribal Enrollment Cards," 1840–1870, 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.

### Treaty & Federal Agency Records
- Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records: annuity payment rolls, correspondence, school records.
- **Where held:** National Archives (main and Fort Worth branch).
- Note: FamilySearch catalog searches under "Oklahoma, United States" returned zero hits — search instead under **"Indian Territory,"** specific tribal nation names, or federal agency names.

### Church / Mission Records
- Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missions were active from the 1820s onward.
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (~123,456 persons) — covers the mid-1800s window.

### Tribal Censuses
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (~567,890 persons) — directly covers the target period.
- No federal decennial census was taken in Indian Territory in this period.

### Land Records
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (~234,567 persons).

### Probate & Court Records
- Tribal nations maintained their own courts; no specific digitized collection was confirmed in this survey — treat as likely physical-only until checked with the National Archives or individual tribal archives.

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Not applicable** for the mid-1800s — there was no civil registration in Indian Territory.
- **Substitutes:** Tribal rolls, mission registers, and BIA agency records fill this gap.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Indian Censuses & Rolls 1851–1959; Land Records 1834–1907; Mission & Church Records 1820–1965; Tribal Enrollment Cards 1840–1870 (image group 002298871) | Free |
| Ancestry | Dawes Rolls and related allotment records | Subscription |
| National Archives (archives.gov) | BIA agency originals, annuity rolls, Dawes Roll originals | Free / in-person or request |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Dawes Rolls, allotment records |
| National Archives (main) | BIA correspondence, annuity rolls, school records |
| Tribal nation archives (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole) | Nation-specific rolls, council and court records — contact each tribe directly |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1851 and 1852 rolls** (Old Settler Cherokee Roll; Drennen Roll) rather than jumping straight to the Dawes Rolls — these are the mid-1800s-specific enrollments.
2. **Cross-reference early rolls with the Dawes Rolls**: because they record blood quantum and tribal affiliation, working both series together reveals family continuity.
3. **BIA annuity payment rolls** often name heads of household or entire families and can substitute for census records in this period.
4. **Mission registers** (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) may record baptisms, marriages, and deaths decades before any civil registration existed.
5. **Catalog searching tip:** Use "Indian Territory" or specific tribal-nation names rather than "Oklahoma, United States" — the modern state place label returns no catalog hits for this period.
6. **Contact tribal archives directly** for nation-level administrative records (tribal council minutes, court records) not held at the National Archives.

---

## Known Gaps in This Survey
- Oklahoma-specific FamilySearch Wiki guide pages could not be retrieved; visit the FamilySearch Wiki directly for Oklahoma and Indian Territory pages.
- Tribal court and probate records: not confirmed as digitized — assume physical-only until verified.
- No confirmed record of losses for this region, but absence of confirmation is not evidence of completeness.

---

**Bottom line:** Because Indian Territory had no counties or civil vital-records registration in the mid-1800s, tribal enrollment rolls, BIA agency papers, and mission church registers are the core substitutes. The Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852) are your starting points; FamilySearch hosts confirmed collections for tribal censuses, land records, and mission records; and original federal agency records sit at the National Archives in Fort Worth.

Here is what the locality-guide found for Pennsylvania Quaker research in the late 1700s:

---

**Pennsylvania Quaker Families — Late 1700s Research Guide**

Pennsylvania had **no civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906, so for Quaker ancestors the monthly meeting records are the essential substitute. Monthly meetings kept detailed minutes covering:

- **Births and deaths**
- **Marriages** (Friends married within the meeting, with witnesses listed)
- **Certificates of removal** — issued when a family relocated to another meeting; these trace migration across counties and states
- **Disownments** — common during the Revolutionary War period for members who took up arms or swore oaths

The densest Quaker populations in this era were in **Chester County**, **Bucks County**, and **Philadelphia**.

---

**Key Repositories and Resources**

| Resource | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** | The single largest repository of Pennsylvania Quaker meeting records |
| **William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 vols.)** | Widely used published abstracts of meeting minutes — useful when originals aren't digitized |
| **FamilySearch Catalog** | Search directly for specific county meeting records; some Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes are digitized but unindexed (must be browsed page by page) |

> **Note:** Searches of the general FamilySearch collections and wiki during this survey returned limited Pennsylvania-specific Quaker results — that reflects a gap in the online lookup, not an absence of surviving records.

---

**Recommended Next Step**

Build a research plan targeting the specific Chester, Bucks, or Philadelphia monthly meeting minutes for your ancestor's location, cross-referencing Hinshaw's abstracts, and following any removal certificates to trace the family as they moved between meetings.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States — Quaker Communities (1750-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States; Pennsylvania as a state dates from 1787 per place_search, though Quaker settlement and meeting structures long predate that.
- **Population during period:** place_population returned no data for this query; not confirmed in this survey.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers) had dense populations in Chester County, Bucks County, and Philadelphia, per the FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Church Records page.
- **Key historical events:** This period spans the American Revolution and early Republic; Quaker meetings' pacifist stance led to disownments of members who took up arms or swore oaths, visible in meeting discipline records.

## Boundary changes
- Not surveyed in detail for this theme; Pennsylvania's county structure (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia) was established well before 1750 and is treated as stable for this guide's purposes.

## Available record types

### Church (Quaker meeting) records
- **What exists:** Monthly meeting minutes recording births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (transfers between meetings), and disownments (disciplinary proceedings); marriage certificates were signed by all attendees. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Church Records — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records
- **Digitized volume found:** volume_search returned one matching volume for this period: imageGroupNumber 001188322, "Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes," covering Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, 1750-1800, 145 images, 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — classified **browse-only images**, must be paged through image by image.
- **Where held:** The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College holds the largest collection of American Quaker records, per the FamilySearch Wiki. FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers (per the same page), and holds the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume named above.
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states — a practical finding aid when an original minute book is not digitized. Source: same FamilySearch Wiki page.
- **Gaps:** catalog_search for Pennsylvania with subject "Quakers" returned zero hits in this survey — a cataloguing gap in this tool, not evidence the records are unavailable; search the FamilySearch Catalog directly and consult Swarthmore's Friends Historical Library.
- **Language:** English.

- Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration requirement until 1906 (per the generic FamilySearch state overview fetched in this survey, which gives this date without naming a level below "statewide"). For 1750-1800, Quaker meeting records substitute for civil vital records.

### Probate and court records
- collections_search returned "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196), overlapping the target period; its personCount came back as 0 in this survey, so indexed-name coverage for 1750-1800 could not be confirmed.
- Quaker meetings sometimes administered their own disciplinary "courts" (meeting for business); county probate and orphans' court records run alongside and should still be checked for wills and estate administrations of Quaker families.

| Repository | Collections for this theme | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (imageGroupNumber 001188322, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950; Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 | Browse-only original minutes; civil-marriage and probate overlap records | Free |
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Largest collection of American Quaker meeting records (per FamilySearch Wiki) | Original/microfilmed meeting minutes beyond what FamilySearch has filmed | Physical/by request |

- The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume (001188322) is online as images only, with 0% name indexing and no full-text search — it must be browsed page by page.
- Monthly meeting minutes for Chester County and Bucks County meetings were not returned by volume_search or collections_search in this survey; check the FamilySearch Catalog and Swarthmore's Friends Historical Library directly for their holdings.

- No tool result in this survey reported destroyed or lost Quaker meeting records for Pennsylvania; none is claimed here.

- Search monthly meeting minutes for births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal, and disownments — a certificate of removal tracks a family's move between meetings and can connect two localities. - Prioritize Chester County, Bucks County, and Philadelphia monthly meetings, the densest Quaker population centers named in this period by the FamilySearch Wiki. Same source.
- Because the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable, plan to browse it image by image rather than relying on a name search.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's generic state-level pages (overview, getting started, online records, research tips) returned only boilerplate U.S.-state content for Pennsylvania in this survey, with no Quaker-specific detail — rely on the Pennsylvania Church Records page instead for this theme.
- Treat a zero-hit catalog_search or an empty collections_search row (such as the Probate Records collection's personCount of 0) as a coverage gap in this survey, not proof the records do not exist — check the FamilySearch Catalog and Swarthmore's Friends Historical Library directly.

Here is the locality guide produced for **Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, 1870–1900**:

---

## Pittsburgh — Tracing Families Through Occupational & Industrial Sources

The late 1800s steel boom drew waves of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian mill workers into Allegheny County. Tracing them requires layering several record types rather than relying on a single source:

### Federal Census Records

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- **County seat:** Pittsburgh.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States.
- **Population during period:** place_population returned no data for this place/period in this run - not confirmed by this survey.
- **Economy:** Pittsburgh became the center of the American steel industry in the late 1800s (Andrew Carnegie's steel empire and other major firms) (Wikipedia, 'Pittsburgh').
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive immigration of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers to the mills (Wikipedia, 'Pittsburgh').
- **Religious denominations:** Many ethnic Catholic parishes (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish) from the 1840s onward (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- **Key historical events:** Rise of Carnegie's steel empire and associated labor immigration waves in the late 1800s (Wikipedia, 'Pittsburgh').

## Boundary changes
This survey found no record of boundary changes to Allegheny County or Pittsburgh during 1870-1900; place_search/place_search_all were not run for historical boundary variants because none were indicated.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level births and deaths recorded in Allegheny County from 1870; marriage licenses from 1885 at the county courthouse (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy'). Statewide civil registration generically began only in the early 1900s per the generic FamilySearch Wiki vital-records page read in this run (no place-specific year given there).
- **What exists:** Births, deaths (from 1870), marriage licenses (from 1885), held at the county courthouse.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Courthouse; FamilySearch's 'Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950' (collection 1921317) and 'Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950' (collection 1571957) cover marriages at the state-indexed level.
- **Gaps:** This survey did not confirm online county-level birth/death indexes for 1870-1900; FamilySearch's 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' (collection 2255317) only starts in 1906, after this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church (parish) baptism, marriage, and burial registers from the 1840s onward.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Ethnic Catholic parishes - Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish - from the 1840s onward (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- **Record types:** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers.
- **Where held:** The Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds many originals.
- **Gaps:** This survey did not confirm online digitization of these parish registers; collections_search did not return a Pittsburgh-specific parish collection (it returned only Pennsylvania-state-level collections).
- **Language:** Records for ethnic parishes may be in languages other than English (e.g., Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian); this survey did not confirm specifics.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Federal census records for Allegheny County survive from 1800; the 1880 and 1900 censuses are especially valuable for industrial workers, recording occupation, parents' birthplace, and (1900) immigration year (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- **State/provincial census:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Access:** This survey did not confirm indexing status for the 1880/1900 Allegheny County census; volume_search returned no county-specific census volumes.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianship files.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not established for any specific ancestor in this survey; search both wills and administrations.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch's 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196, person_count 0 - i.e., unindexed) spans this period; volume_search found a matching browse-only probate volume (image group 008120441, 1,180 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Where held:** County courthouse originals; FamilySearch holds a browse-only digitized volume (no name index).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed by this survey - the {Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property wiki page was not reached (place_page sections returned only generic content).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records - not detailed further by this run's tool results.
- **Where held:** County recorder of deeds (by convention; not separately confirmed this run).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** None specific to 1870-1900 confirmed by this survey (post-Civil War, pre-Spanish-American War mobilization not detailed).
- **Record types:** Not detailed by this run's tool results.
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA), per external_links_search result.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/), per external_links_search.
- **Physical records:** Not confirmed by this survey.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Not named by this survey.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/), per external_links_search.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices likely, not separately confirmed.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Pittsburgh is inland; immigrants to the steel mills typically arrived via East Coast ports (not specified by this run's tool results) and then migrated inland.
- **Record types:** Naturalization petitions - Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records (1798-1930) are held at the National Archives at Philadelphia (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy'). volume_search also found a Pennsylvania-level naturalization volume (image group 008120443, 351 images, 15% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in English and German).
- **Where held:** National Archives at Philadelphia; NARA generally (https://www.archives.gov/).
- **Content note:** Review full passenger manifests for all family members when located.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Not detailed by this run's tool results.
- **Date range:** Not confirmed.
- **Where held:** County courthouse (by convention).
- **Substitute value:** Could substitute for missing 1890 census (destroyed nationally), not separately confirmed for this county.

### Other record types (occupational/industrial)
- Company and mill employment records, union membership lists, and city directories are the key occupational sources for steelworker ancestors; the Heinz History Center houses extensive industrial and immigration records relevant to Pittsburgh's steel workforce (Wikipedia, 'Pittsburgh').
- Pittsburgh city directories begin in 1813 and are held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy') - useful between census years to track occupation and address changes.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 (1,048,378 people); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 (unindexed, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (624,090 people); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (397,530 people) | Marriage coverage 1885-1900; browse-only probate access | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1880/1900 federal census access | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | No county-level sexton/cemetery records confirmed online this run | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | No local obituary/marriage-notice index confirmed this run | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | No period-specific (1870-1900) Allegheny County military record confirmed this run | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Naturalization and passenger-list originals | Free (in-person) / some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 3 total digitized volumes at the Pennsylvania state level for 1870-1900 (probate, death, and naturalization), described as the complete result set for that query (complete: true); none were Allegheny-County-specific, and catalog_search returned 0 hits at both the county and state levels, so this is a coverage gap in this run rather than a claim that no catalog holdings exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Birth/death records from 1870, marriage licenses from 1885, probate and court records | In-person / mail request |
| Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Original ethnic-parish baptism, marriage, and burial registers (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish parishes) | In-person / written request |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from 1813 | In-person / library access |
| Heinz History Center | Industrial and immigration records relevant to the steel workforce | In-person |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records, 1798-1930 | In-person / written request |

## Records NOT online
Parish registers held by the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives, company/mill employment records, union membership records, and Carnegie Library city directories are not confirmed as available in any online database by this survey - treat them as physical-repository-only unless confirmed otherwise.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this run states that any specific Allegheny County or Pittsburgh record series was destroyed or lost; this is not confirmed either way by this survey.

## Research tips
- Search ethnic Catholic parish registers by specific parish and ethnicity (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish), not just by city, since Pittsburgh's many ethnic parishes kept separate registers from the 1840s onward (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- Use the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses specifically for industrial-worker ancestors: they record occupation, parents' birthplace, and (1900 only) immigration year (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- Use Pittsburgh city directories (from 1813, at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh) to track a worker's occupation and address between census years (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- Check the Heinz History Center for company, union, and immigration records specific to the steel industry workforce (Wikipedia, 'Pittsburgh').
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, not only the county court - check the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas records (1798-1930) at the National Archives at Philadelphia (FamilySearch Wiki, 'Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy').
- The FamilySearch Wiki's four standard place-research pages (home, getting started, online records, research tips) returned only generic content for this place in this run - re-run this survey, or consult the Wiki directly, to try to get place-specific editions of those pages.

Here is the locality guide produced for Philadelphia and the 1793 yellow fever epidemic:

---

**Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic: Records & Repositories**

Since Pennsylvania had no civil registration until 1906, there is no single official death register to consult. The records that actually document this outbreak fall into several categories:

### Key Record Types

1. **Church Burial and Baptismal Registers**
   - Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal) and Gloria Dei "Old Swedes'" Church are among the congregations known to have recorded burials during the epidemic. Many other Philadelphia congregations kept similar registers. These vary in survival, digitization, and access — contact each church archive or the denomination's regional repository directly.

2. **Mathew Carey's Published List of the Dead**
   - A contemporary printed list of victims was compiled by Mathew Carey during the epidemic. This is a primary finding aid for deaths during that specific period.

3. **Committee Minutes and Relief Records**
   - A citizens' relief committee organized aid during the crisis. Its minutes and reports name individuals who received or administered relief — useful for locating families even if they did not die.

4. **Bush Hill Fever Hospital Records**
   - The temporary hospital at Bush Hill served many of the ill. Any surviving patient or administrative records would be held in institutional archives.

5. **Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting) Records**
   - A browse-only, unindexed volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes covering 1750–1800 was found in the digitized catalog — not name-indexed, but browsable for researchers with Quaker ancestry.

### Repositories to Approach Directly

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | Municipal records, committee records, hospital records |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Manuscript collections, Carey's list, relief committee papers |
| **Individual church archives** | Burial and baptismal registers |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society** | Presbyterian congregational records |

### Important Caveat

Catalog and collection searches for pre-indexed Philadelphia yellow fever material came back empty — meaning most of these records **have not been digitized or put online** in a searchable form. A researcher should expect to write to or visit the archives and congregations rather than rely on remote searching.

### Suggested Next Steps

- Contact the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** (hsp.org) for their manuscript holdings related to 1793.
- Contact **Philadelphia City Archives** for civic records from the period.
- Identify the specific congregation(s) your ancestors belonged to and locate that church's archive.
- Obtain a copy of **Mathew Carey's** published account and list of the dead (*A Short Account of the Malignant Fever*, 1793) — available in some digitized library collections.

Would you like a concrete research plan built from this guide, or help locating a specific record type or repository?

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic, 1780-1810)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia City and County have existed since 1682 (per place_search, dateRange +1682/); no formation event falls in the target period.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Wikipedia reports roughly 50,000 residents in 1793, of whom approximately 5,000 (about one-tenth) died in the epidemic (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). place_population returned no data for this place in this survey.
- **Economy:** Major port and the then-capital of the United States.
- **Key historical events:** The yellow fever epidemic of August-November 1793, which killed an estimated 5,000 people and caused mass flight from the city (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793).

## Boundary changes
No boundary change affecting Philadelphia City/County is indicated for this period by place_search; the city and county share the same founding date range in the tool's data.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Not stated for Philadelphia specifically by any page reachable in this survey; the general FamilySearch guidance fetched (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) says many U.S. states, including Pennsylvania, did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s -- the collections_search result 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' is consistent with that and confirms civil death registration had not begun in 1793.
- **What exists:** No civil vital registration for 1793; see Church records below for the period's actual source.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial and baptismal registers (Wikipedia names Christ Church, Gloria Dei/Old Swedes', and other Philadelphia congregations as having recorded burials during the epidemic).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Wikipedia's summary of the epidemic names Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') congregations as keeping burial records of the dead in 1793; it also notes other, unnamed church archives hold burial/death records from the epidemic.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1871, Great Chicago Fire)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **County seat:** Chicago is the county seat of Cook County, established 1831.
- **Key event:** The Great Chicago Fire burned October 8–10, 1871, killed roughly 300 people, destroyed ~3.3 square miles, left 100,000+ homeless, and — critically for genealogists — destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which held deeds, birth/death registers, court records, and tax rolls (per Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire).

---

## Boundary Changes
No boundary changes for Chicago/Cook County in this period. The 1871 disruption was to *records*, not jurisdiction.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- Cook County vital registration collections on FamilySearch begin **exactly in 1871** — consistent with the courthouse fire destroying all earlier records:
  - **Birth Certificates, 1871–1940** (collection id 2024189)
  - **Death Records, 1871–1947** (collection id 1913456)
  - **Marriage Records, 1871–1920** (collection id 1756321)
- **Pre-fire gap:** No surviving civil vital registers pre-1871 are confirmed in this survey.
- **Held at:** Cook County Clerk's office (originals from 1871 onward).

### Church Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" (id 1803978) — spans both before and after the fire, making it a key pre-fire substitute.
- **Catholic records:** Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds parish registers.
- **Caveat:** Some church registers were also lost in the fire; which specific congregations survived is not confirmed by any tool result in this survey.

### Census Records
- The **1850, 1860, and 1870 federal census schedules** for Chicago survived because originals were held in Washington — not destroyed locally. The 1870 census is the most critical pre-fire household snapshot.
- Access via Ancestry.com's U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and Court Records
- Pre-fire wills, estate files, and court records were largely destroyed with the courthouse.
- FamilySearch has a surviving digitized volume: **"Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies), 1865–1871"** (image group 009982110) — 38 images, 0% name-indexed, **browse-only**.

### Land Records
- Pre-fire deeds destroyed. The **1872 Burnt Record Act** required property owners to re-register their deeds.
- FamilySearch digitized volume: **"Post-fire Property Re-recordings, 1871–1880"** (image group 009982111) — 112 images, **41% name-indexed** (the other 59% requires browse-only image-by-image review).
- **Key substitute:** Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records held at the **Chicago History Museum** — a primary substitute for pre-fire property ownership.

### Military Records
- Civil War service/pension files (1861–65) predate the fire and are unaffected by courthouse loss. Held at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).

### Newspapers
- Chicago newspaper coverage of the fire itself may include casualty lists, missing-persons notices, and relief rolls — pursue via Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/). No specific confirmed title/date range was returned by tools in this survey.

---

## Known Record Losses
The courthouse fire destroyed:
- Civil birth, death, and marriage registers (pre-1871)
- Deeds and land records
- Court and probate files
- Tax rolls
- Many church registers

**Survived because held outside Chicago:** 1850, 1860, and 1870 federal census schedules.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Vital records from 1871, church records 1833–1925, reconstructed court records (browse-only), post-fire property re-recordings (partly indexed) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1850/1860/1870 schedules survive) | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery/burial information | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Local papers, obituaries, fire-era notices | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service/pension records | Subscription |
| **NARA** | Federal originals: census, military, naturalization | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** | City directories from 1840s onward (survived the fire), maps, manuscripts |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records, photos, personal papers |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (Northeastern Illinois University)** | Cook County records post-1871 |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago, Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — it survived (copy held in Washington) and places households immediately before the fire.
2. **Use the Burnt Record Act re-recordings** (FamilySearch vol. 009982111, 41% indexed) for post-fire property ownership; browse the unindexed 59% image-by-image.
3. **Browse the reconstructed court records** (vol. 009982110) image-by-image — 0% indexed, no name search available.
4. **Chicago History Museum** is the primary destination for pre-fire property ownership evidence via insurance/title company records.
5. **City directories at the Newberry Library** (1840s onward) are a valuable pre-fire name and address source that survived.
6. **Church records (1833–1925 collection)** are the main pre-fire substitute for vital events — but be aware some registers were also lost.
7. FamilySearch's Catalog search for Cook County, Illinois returned zero hits during this survey — check the catalog directly at familysearch.org, as the tool gap may underrepresent available microfilm holdings.

---

The next logical step would be building a research plan starting with the 1870 census and the post-fire re-recorded deeds, then filling gaps with church records and city directories.

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1871, Great Chicago Fire)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County was established in 1831; Chicago is its county seat and largest city. No boundary change affects the 1871 period.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** Not confirmed by this survey — `place_population` returned no data for Cook County for this lookup; could not be verified here.
- **Economy:** Rapidly industrializing rail/commercial hub in 1871, which is part of why the fire's record loss was so consequential (courthouse at the civic/commercial core).
- **Key historical event:** The Great Chicago Fire burned October 8–10, 1871, killed roughly 300 people, destroyed about 3.3 square miles, and left over 100,000 homeless. It destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls, per Wikipedia's "Great Chicago Fire" article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire).

## Boundary changes
Boundaries were unchanged for Chicago/Cook County across this period; the disruption in 1871 was to *records*, not jurisdiction.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** FamilySearch's wiki content returned to this survey's `Illinois_Vital_Records` request was generic boilerplate (actual URL served back was "Genealogy_Records", https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records), so this survey cannot confirm the year or level Illinois/Cook County vital registration began.
- **What exists:** `collections_search` (scope: Illinois) returned Cook County collections beginning exactly in 1871 — "Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871-1940" (id 2024189), "Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871-1947" (id 1913456), and "Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871-1920" (id 1756321) — all starting the fire year, consistent with the courthouse loss.
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office holds vital records from 1871 onward, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- **Gaps:** Pre-fire civil vital registers for Chicago/Cook County were destroyed with the courthouse; no online collection in this survey covers vital events before 1871.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers from parishes that survived or were re-established, per the same wiki result.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Not itemized by a tool result for specific denominations beyond "Church Records" generally.
- **Record types:** FamilySearch collection "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833-1925" (id 1803978) spans well before and after the fire, making it a key pre-fire substitute.
- **Where held:** Catholic parish registers are held at the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives, per the wiki search result above. No tool result in this survey assigns any specific pre-1871 congregation to a named parish — do not infer one.
- **Gaps:** Some church registers were also lost in the fire ("many church registers" destroyed, per the same wiki excerpt); which specific congregations survived is not stated by any tool result here.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, and 1870 federal schedules for Chicago survived the fire because the originals were held in Washington, per the FamilySearch Wiki search excerpt (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). This makes the 1870 census a critical pre-fire household snapshot.
- **Other enumerations:** Not confirmed by a tool result for this place/period.
- **Access:** `collections_search` did not return a dedicated census collection row for this place in this survey; use the general federal census collections (see Repository guide).

- **Where held:** Not stated beyond the FamilySearch digitized volume above; `catalog_search` for Cook County, Illinois returned zero hits in this survey (a cataloguing gap, not evidence the records don't exist).

### Land records
- **Context:** Deeds and property records were destroyed in the fire. The 1872 Burnt Record Act required property owners to re-register their deeds, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire).
- **Records found:** `volume_search` returned image group 009982111, "Post-fire Property Re-recordings," 1871–1880, 112 images, 41% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — partially searchable, otherwise browse the remainder image by image.

### Military records
- Not surveyed in tool detail here beyond the general guidance that service, pension, and draft records are held at NARA (per the generic FamilySearch guide page returned, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records). Civil War service/pension files (1861–65) would predate the fire and are unaffected by the courthouse loss.

### Cemetery records

- No specific Chicago newspaper title or date range was returned by any tool in this survey. Newspapers.com is listed in curated external links (below) as a general resource; Chicago papers covering the fire itself (reporting on casualties, missing persons, relief rolls) would be a secondary-source lead worth pursuing there, but no specific title/run is confirmed here.

### Immigration/emigration records

No Chicago-specific port-of-entry collection was returned (Chicago was not itself a NARA passenger-arrival port in this era in the national immigration framework — the Great Lakes ports of New York etc. were the entry points for most Chicago immigrants).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871-1940" (id 2024189), "Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871-1947" (id 1913456), "Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871-1920" (id 1756321), "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833-1925" (id 1803978), digitized volumes 009982110 (pre-fire court records, reconstructed copies) and 009982111 (post-fire property re-recordings) | Vital records only from 1871; church records bridge the pre/post-fire gap; the two digitized volumes are the direct fire-related record sets | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library | City directories (1840s onward survived the fire), maps, manuscripts, per the FamilySearch wiki search result | In-person / contact library |
| Chicago History Museum | Insurance company records (notably Chicago Title and Trust Company), photographs, personal papers | In-person / contact museum |

| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | In-person / contact archives |

## Records NOT online
Pre-fire Cook County deeds, probate files, and most pre-fire court/tax records exist today only as the reconstructed/re-recorded paper and microfilm series noted above (where they survive at all) — the underlying originals were destroyed. The Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records and city directories held at the Newberry Library and Chicago History Museum are not confirmed as digitized by any tool result in this survey; treat them as physical-repository-only until verified otherwise.

## Known record losses
The Cook County Courthouse fire in October 1871 destroyed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire), and "many church registers" were also lost, per the FamilySearch Wiki search excerpt (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). The 1850, 1860, and 1870 federal census schedules for Chicago survived because the originals were held in Washington rather than locally, per the same source. Substitute sources: the 1872 Burnt Record Act re-recorded deeds (see the 41%-indexed volume above); insurance/title company records at the Chicago History Museum; surviving/re-established church registers (1833–1925 collection); city directories at the Newberry Library.

## Research tips

I looked at records for Chicago, Illinois around the time of the 1871 Great Fire. The fire destroyed the county courthouse along with most birth, death, marriage, deed, and court records up to that point, so family history before 1871 has to be pieced together from substitutes: the 1850, 1860, and 1870 census (which survived because copies were kept in Washington), church baptism/marriage/burial registers (some of which also burned, but FamilySearch has a surviving collection from 1833 onward), old insurance and title-company records held at the Chicago History Museum, and city directories at the Newberry Library. After the fire, property owners had to formally re-file their deeds, and FamilySearch has a partly searchable, partly browse-only set of those re-filings, plus new vital records that only start in 1871; several of the official FamilySearch Wiki pages for this specific county could not be retrieved with place-specific detail during this search, so some local specifics should be double-checked directly on that site.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

French Louisiana (1682–1762) was an administrative district of New France. By the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau, west-of-the-Mississippi territory (including New Orleans) passed secretly to Spain, while east-of-the-Mississippi passed to Britain in 1763. Spain retroceded to France in 1800; Napoleon sold the territory to the United States in 1803.

- **Administrative center:** New Orleans, founded 1718
- **Religion:** Roman Catholicism was the only legally recognized church — this is critical for record types
- **Population:** French settlers, enslaved Africans (the Code Noir required Catholic baptism), and Native Americans

---

## Key Record Types and Where to Find Them

### 1. Catholic Church Records *(primary vital-record substitute)*
Since there was **no secular civil registration** in French colonial Louisiana, the Catholic Church is your main source for births (baptisms), marriages, and burials.

- **St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans** holds registers from **1720**
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, ~987,654 persons) — indexed, searchable by name
- **FamilySearch Digitized Volume:** Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans (image group 004330991, 264 images, **1720–1803**, browse-only, 0% name-indexed, in French and Spanish)
- **Language warning:** Registers are in French (and later Spanish) — must be read in the original language

---

### 2. Superior Council / Notarial Records *(legal, land, estate records)*
The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) kept land grants, court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories.

- **FamilySearch Digitized Volume:** "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)" (image group 004330992, 149 images, **1699–1769**, browse-only, 0% indexed, French/Spanish)
- **Physical repository:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans — only partially digitized; the rest requires in-person access

---

### 3. Probate and Notarial Records
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds the oldest continuous notarial office in North America, with holdings from the **1730s** onward (wills, marriage settlements, property contracts, estate inventories)
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341) — covers the late colonial period; note it only begins in **1756**, so pre-1756 material must be sought at the Notarial Archives in person

---

### 4. Land Records
- French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the **American State Papers: Public Lands** series
- **Louisiana State Land Office** (in-person or records request)
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives** for property contracts
- Survey system follows French and Spanish legal traditions — not English common law

---

### 5. Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), France *(critical overseas repository)*
The **ANOM in Aix-en-Provence, France** holds administrative correspondence and census rolls for French colonial Louisiana — material not held in Louisiana itself. This is an essential repository for colonial-era research not reachable through U.S. archives.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Church records 1718–1925; probate records 1756–1984; digitized browse-only sacramental registers and Superior Council notarial acts | Free |
| Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans) | Superior Council records (partially digitized) | In-person |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from the 1730s onward | In-person |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Administrative records and census rolls for French colonial Louisiana | In-person / ANOM access channels |
| St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans | Sacramental registers from 1720 | Parish archive (partially on FamilySearch) |
| Louisiana State Land Office | French concessions and Spanish land grants | In-person / records request |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Use Catholic parish registers as your vital-records substitute** — no secular birth/marriage/death registration existed under French colonial rule.
2. **Browse-only volumes require patience:** The FamilySearch digitized volumes for sacramental registers and Superior Council acts are 0% name-indexed — you must page through them image by image and read French or Spanish.
3. **Don't stop at U.S. archives** — the ANOM in France holds administrative and census material absent from Louisiana repositories.
4. **For probate/notarial records before 1756**, go directly to the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, as FamilySearch's probate collection only begins in 1756.
5. **Language:** Colonial records are in French (pre-1769) and Spanish (1769–1800); be prepared to read in those languages or find translation assistance.

---

*No project was open during this survey, so nothing was saved to a research file. If you have a specific ancestor in mind, the next step would be to create a project and build a research plan targeting these record sets.*

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French colonial period, 1699-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** French Louisiana was an administrative district of New France, 1682-1762 (east of the Mississippi passed to Britain in 1763; west of the Mississippi, including New Orleans, passed to Spain by the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau), per Wikipedia's "French Louisiana" article. Spain secretly retroceded the colony to France in 1800, and Napoleon sold it to the United States in 1803.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans, founded 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville (Wikipedia).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Administered under New France until 1762/1763; thereafter under Spain (1762-1800) for most of the territory.
- **Economy/ethnic composition:** Colonial Louisiana included French settlers, enslaved Africans (the Code Noir governed slavery and required Catholic baptism of enslaved people), and Native American populations, per Wikipedia and a FamilySearch Wiki search result on "Louisiana Genealogy."
- **Religious denominations:** The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Louisiana Genealogy," French Colonial Records section).
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); transfer of governance from France to Spain (1762/1769); retrocession to France (1800) and the Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary changes
French Louisiana's territory was split in 1762-1763 (west of the Mississippi to Spain, east to Britain), administered by Spain until 1800, then briefly French again before the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. Civil and notarial record-keeping continued across these transfers under the Superior Council (French era) and then Spanish colonial administration — later records may be filed under either regime's naming conventions, so searches should not assume a single continuous jurisdictional name through the century.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
During the French colonial period there was no secular civil-registration system comparable to later U.S. statewide registration; the Catholic Church was the de facto recorder of births (via baptism), marriages, and deaths (via burial) (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Louisiana Genealogy"). Treat church sacramental registers, below, as the primary vital-record substitute for this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only, as the sole legally recognized church (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Louisiana Genealogy").
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans holds registers from 1720 (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Louisiana Genealogy," French Colonial Records section).
- **Where held:** `volume_search` found a digitized, browse-only volume of "Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans," covering Orleans, Louisiana, 1720-1803 (image group 004330991, 264 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and Spanish). FamilySearch's indexed collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905, ~987,654 persons) also spans this period.
- **Language:** French (and later Spanish) — registers are not in English; the researcher must read the original language.
- **Gaps:** No wiki page specifically on Louisiana church records could be retrieved with place-specific content in this survey (see gap note below); rely on the collections and volume named above.

### Court / Superior Council records
The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) kept land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories; these are held at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans, and are partially digitized (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Louisiana Genealogy"). `volume_search` found a matching browse-only, non-indexed volume: "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)," covering Louisiana, 1699-1769 (image group 004330992, 149 images, French/Spanish, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable).

### Probate and notarial records
- **Types:** Wills, marriage settlements, property contracts, estate inventories.
- **Where held:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds the records of the oldest continuous notarial office in North America, with holdings from the 1730s onward (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Louisiana Land and Property"). FamilySearch's indexed "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341, ~456,789 persons) overlaps the tail of the colonial period.
- **Date range:** From the 1730s per the Notarial Archives; the FamilySearch probate collection begins 1756.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French and Spanish legal land-grant traditions, not English common law (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Louisiana Land and Property").
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial-era concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office (same source).
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial property contracts.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Land Office; American State Papers (printed series); New Orleans Notarial Archives.

### Archival records abroad
Administrative correspondence and census rolls for the French colony are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France (FamilySearch Wiki search result, "Louisiana Genealogy"). This is the key repository for colonial administrative material not held in Louisiana itself.

### Census records
No census-specific collection or volume for the 1700s was returned by this survey's tools. The Superior Council's administrative records and the ANOM census rolls noted above are the identified substitutes; no U.S. federal census applies before 1790, and no 1790-era Louisiana state/territorial enumeration was confirmed by this survey.

### Military, cemetery, newspaper, immigration and tax records
No colonial-period-specific volumes, collections, or wiki content for these record types in Louisiana were returned by this survey's tools. `external_links_search` returned only generic national resources (Ancestry's general census collection, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) with no Louisiana-specific curated links among them — these are starting points, not confirmed Louisiana colonial-era holdings.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection 1612905, ~987,654 persons); "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection 2078341, ~456,789 persons); digitized browse-only sacramental registers (image group 004330991) and Superior Council notarial acts (image group 004330992) | Catholic sacramental and notarial substitutes for absent civil vital/land registration | Free |
| Ancestry.com | General U.S. Federal Census Collection (no colonial Louisiana-specific collection confirmed) | — | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (general) | — | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (general) | — | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (general) | — | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives general holdings | — | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 total digitized volumes for Louisiana, 1699-1803, and both are detailed above (no further pages exist). `collections_search` returned 4 total FamilySearch collections for Louisiana; all 4 are listed, though only two overlap the colonial window. `catalog_search` on "Louisiana, United States" returned 0 hits — a cataloguing gap in this survey, not evidence that catalog holdings (e.g., for the Superior Council or ANOM materials) do not exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records: land concessions, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories | In-person |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from the 1730s onward: contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions | In-person, public access |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Administrative correspondence and census rolls for French colonial Louisiana | In-person or via ANOM's own access channels (not detailed by this survey's tools) |
| St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans | Sacramental registers from 1720 | Parish archive; also partially reflected in the FamilySearch digitized volume above |
| Louisiana State Land Office | French concessions and Spanish land grants | In-person / records request |

## Records NOT online
The Superior Council records at the Louisiana Historical Center are described as only "partially digitized" — the remainder exists only in that physical repository. The ANOM administrative correspondence and census rolls are not reflected in any FamilySearch collection or volume returned by this survey and so must be accessed through ANOM directly. The New Orleans Notarial Archives' pre-1756 holdings (back to the 1730s) are not covered by the FamilySearch "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" collection, which starts in 1756.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey reported a specific record loss, destruction, or gap for French colonial Louisiana; the absence of census or military-record volumes for this period is a coverage gap in the tools used, not a stated loss. Treat the sacramental and notarial substitutes above as the primary extant sources rather than assuming a confirmed destruction.

## Research tips
- The sacramental registers and Superior Council notarial acts digitized by FamilySearch are entirely browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and in French and Spanish — you must browse image by image and read the original language.
- Treat Catholic parish baptism, marriage, and burial registers as your vital-records substitute for this period, since no secular civil registration existed under French colonial rule, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result on Louisiana Genealogy.
- Check the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in France for administrative correspondence and census rolls not held in Louisiana itself.
- Consult the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center directly for contracts, wills, and property records from the 1730s onward, since FamilySearch's indexed probate collection only begins in 1756.
- This survey's attempts to fetch Louisiana-specific FamilySearch Wiki pages (home, getting-started, online-records, research-tips, and constructed URLs for Louisiana Vital Records and Louisiana Church Records) each returned only generic template content with no Louisiana-specific detail — treat those as pages worth checking manually on the FamilySearch Wiki site itself, since this survey could not confirm their content.
- `catalog_search` and `place_population` returned no results for Louisiana in this survey; do not conclude from this that no catalog or population data exists — it indicates a gap in this survey's tool coverage.

No project was given, so nothing was saved to a research file.

---
This survey looked at Louisiana during the 1700s, the era when it was a French (and later Spanish) colony rather than a U.S. state, and found that family records from that time mostly come from the Catholic Church, since it was the only legally recognized religion and the government had no separate system for recording births, marriages, and deaths. Key places to look are old Catholic parish registers (such as those of St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans, with records from 1720), colonial government and notarial records kept in New Orleans archives, and French government archival material held overseas in France; several of these old church and notarial pages exist as digitized but unindexed images, meaning they must be browsed page by page and read in French or Spanish rather than searched by name, and a genealogy wiki search specifically meant to describe these record types for Louisiana did not return usable detail, so some of it may need to be checked by hand on the FamilySearch website. The next step would be to build a research plan that uses these record sets to search for your specific ancestors.

Here is what the survey found for **Pennsylvania anthracite coal country (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties), 1850–1900**:

---

## Key Finding: Civil Registration Came Late

Pennsylvania had **no statewide requirement** for recording births, marriages, and deaths until **1906** (Philadelphia started in 1860, Allegheny County in 1870). That means for the late 1800s, **church registers are your primary source** for vital events — not a state vital records office.

---

## Records & Repositories

### Church Records
- The main source for births, marriages, and deaths in this era
- Many immigrant mining families were Catholic, Welsh Calvinist Methodist, or various Protestant denominations
- Church registers may be held at individual parishes or deposited at diocesan archives

### County Courthouse Records
- **Marriage licenses**, **deeds**, and **probate/will records** were always kept at the county level
- Target the county courthouse for the specific county where your family lived

### Mine-Specific Records
- **Schuylkill County**: Digitized mine-worker employment cards are **name-searchable online**
- **Luzerne County**: Mine accident reports — digitized but only browsable by image, no name index
- **Lackawanna County**: Colliery payroll ledgers — same situation, image-browse only

### Key Repositories (In-Person or Limited Online Access)
| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Statewide mining and government records |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Local mining-community records |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) | Mining-community records for the Lackawanna area |

### Other Record Types
- **Land, tax, and cemetery records** for this area turned up no confirmed online collections — these remain open gaps to investigate further, not confirmed absences

---

## Important Note on County Lines

Mining families frequently moved between collieries across county lines. It is worth checking **all five counties** (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland) rather than limiting the search to just one.

---

## Recommended Next Step

A research plan can be built from this survey to target specific ancestors and record sets. If you share the county where your family is believed to have lived, we can prioritize those record sets and repositories.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1850-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- Covers Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties, Pennsylvania (per Wikipedia's Coal Region article). Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 (place_search).
- Economy: anthracite coal mining, expanding 1820s-1870s.
- Ethnic composition: large immigrant populations from Ireland, Wales, Germany, and later Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Italy, Ukraine (Wikipedia).
- Mining companies kept employment records, pay ledgers, and accident reports; the Pennsylvania State Archives holds Mine Inspector reports from 1870 (Wikipedia, Coal Region).

## Boundary changes
- This survey covered Schuylkill County only in detail; place_search_all returned no additional historical jurisdictions for it. Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties were not separately surveyed and would need their own locality-guide runs.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Start date: Pennsylvania required no statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906; Philadelphia required it from 1860 and Allegheny County from 1870 (FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Vital Records", https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records).
- Marriage records were kept at the county courthouse from the colonial period (same page).
- Pre-1906 alternative: church records.
- Gap: the direct wiki_read of the Pennsylvania Vital Records URL returned only a generic template page in this survey; the date information above comes from the wiki_search excerpt of that page, not a fully-loaded page read.

### Church records
- Churches recorded vital events before 1906 statewide civil registration (FamilySearch Wiki excerpt above).
- FamilySearch collections_search returned "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985, 982,415 people).
- Denominations are not itemized by any tool result in this survey; this is a gap.

### Census records
- Federal census: no county-specific collection was returned by collections_search; use the standard federal decennial census (1850-1900).
- No state/provincial census or other enumeration was returned for this place in this survey.

### Probate and court records
- collections_search returned "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196, person_count 0 in this result -- likely an index without a linked name count).
- Held at the county Register of Wills per the FamilySearch wiki_read generic Genealogy_Records page.

### Land records
- No Schuylkill-specific land collection was returned by collections_search in this survey; this is a coverage gap, not evidence land records don't exist.
- General PA land records (deeds, patents) are held at county courthouses and the state Land Office per the generic wiki_read page.

### Military records
- No specific collection returned; standard NARA service/pension records apply for the Civil War era within this window.

### Cemetery records
- No cemetery-specific collection returned by collections_search; external_links_search returned Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) as an online cemetery-records resource.

### Newspaper records
- external_links_search returned Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) as a newspaper resource; no Schuylkill-specific title or date range was returned.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not specifically returned by any tool in this survey; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) was returned by external_links_search as a general repository.

### Tax records
- No tax-record collection was returned for this place in this survey; this is a coverage gap.

### Occupational/mining records
- volume_search returned three digitized volumes for the coal region, 1870-1900: Mine Worker Employment Cards (imageGroupNumber 002240015, Schuylkill, 1870-1900, 410 images, 95% record-searchable, full-text searchable); Mine Accident Reports (002240016, Luzerne, 1870-1895, 287 images, 0% record-searchable, not full-text searchable -- browse-only); Colliery Payroll Ledgers (002240017, Lackawanna, 1878-1900, 199 images, 0% record-searchable, not full-text searchable -- browse-only). totalResults for the search was 23 with a nextPageToken (PA_COAL_REGION_PAGE_2) -- only 3 of 23 matching volumes were detailed above; the rest were not examined in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Schuylkill Church Records (982,415 people); PA County Marriages 1885-1950; PA Probate Records 1683-1994; PA Death Certificates 1906-1968; PA Civil Marriages 1677-1950; PA Compiled Marriages 1700-1900; digitized Mine Worker Employment Cards (002240015) | pre-1906 vital-record gap (church records); probate; marriages; mining employment | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection, https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ | federal census | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | https://www.findagrave.com/ | cemetery/burial records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | https://www.newspapers.com/ | obituaries/notices | Subscription |
| Fold3 | https://www.fold3.com/ | military records | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | immigration, military, federal records | Free |

Coverage of this survey: volume_search found 23 digitized volumes matching Pennsylvania/1870-1900; only 3 were detailed above as the first page (a nextPageToken was returned), so most matching volumes were not examined.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania State Archives | Mine Inspector reports from 1870 (Wikipedia, Coal Region) | In-person / written request |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Mining community records (Wikipedia, Coal Region) | Contact directly |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton | Mining community records (Wikipedia, Coal Region) | In-person |
| County courthouse (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland) | Marriage licenses/bonds, deeds, probate | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne, 1870-1895) and Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna, 1878-1900) are digitized but browse-only (0% record-searchable, not full-text searchable) -- no name index, must be browsed image by image.
- Land, tax, and cemetery records for this place returned no online collection in this survey; treat as likely physical-only at the county courthouse pending further search.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey states that any specific record series for this place was destroyed or lost. This absence should not be read as a statement that no losses occurred; it is simply not confirmed here.

## Research tips
- Church registers are the primary vital-records source for 1850-1900, since Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration until 1906 (FamilySearch Wiki excerpt, Pennsylvania Vital Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records).
- Search county courthouses for marriage licenses/bonds, which were recorded at the county level throughout this period (same page).
- Search adjoining coal counties (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland) together, since mining families moved between collieries across county lines (Wikipedia, Coal Region).
- Use mine employment, payroll, and accident records as occupational substitutes/supplements when vital records are unavailable -- the Mine Worker Employment Cards volume is indexed and full-text searchable; the Mine Accident Reports and Colliery Payroll Ledgers volumes are browse-only.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's four place-oriented research pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only a generic template for this place in this survey, not place-specific content -- treat PA-specific tips beyond the Vital Records excerpt above as unconfirmed, and re-check the live FamilySearch Wiki directly.
- catalog_search returned zero hits for Schuylkill County in this survey -- a cataloguing gap, not evidence the county has no microfilmed/physical holdings.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1850-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- Covers Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties, Pennsylvania (per Wikipedia's Coal Region article). Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 (place_search).
- Economy: anthracite coal mining, expanding 1820s-1870s.
- Ethnic composition: large immigrant populations from Ireland, Wales, Germany, and later Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Italy, Ukraine (Wikipedia).
- Mining companies kept employment records, pay ledgers, and accident reports; the Pennsylvania State Archives holds Mine Inspector reports from 1870 (Wikipedia, Coal Region).

## Boundary changes
- This survey covered Schuylkill County only in detail; place_search_all returned no additional historical jurisdictions for it. Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties were not separately surveyed and would need their own locality-guide runs.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Start date: Pennsylvania required no statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906; Philadelphia required it from 1860 and Allegheny County from 1870 (FamilySearch Wiki, "Pennsylvania Vital Records", https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records).
- Marriage records were kept at the county courthouse from the colonial period (same page).
- Pre-1906 alternative: church records.
- Gap: the direct wiki_read of the Pennsylvania Vital Records URL returned only a generic template page in this survey; the date information above comes from the wiki_search excerpt of that page, not a fully-loaded page read.

### Church records
- Churches recorded vital events before 1906 statewide civil registration (FamilySearch Wiki excerpt above).
- FamilySearch collections_search returned "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985, 982,415 people).
- Denominations are not itemized by any tool result in this survey; this is a gap.

### Census records
- Federal census: no county-specific collection was returned by collections_search; use the standard federal decennial census (1850-1900).
- No state/provincial census or other enumeration was returned for this place in this survey.

### Probate and court records
- collections_search returned "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196, person_count 0 in this result -- likely an index without a linked name count).
- Held at the county Register of Wills per the FamilySearch wiki_read generic Genealogy_Records page.

### Land records
- No Schuylkill-specific land collection was returned by collections_search in this survey; this is a coverage gap, not evidence land records don't exist.
- General PA land records (deeds, patents) are held at county courthouses and the state Land Office per the generic wiki_read page.

### Military records
- No specific collection returned; standard NARA service/pension records apply for the Civil War era within this window.

### Cemetery records
- No cemetery-specific collection returned by collections_search; external_links_search returned Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) as an online cemetery-records resource.

### Newspaper records
- external_links_search returned Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) as a newspaper resource; no Schuylkill-specific title or date range was returned.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not specifically returned by any tool in this survey; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) was returned by external_links_search as a general repository.

### Tax records
- No tax-record collection was returned for this place in this survey; this is a coverage gap.

### Occupational/mining records
- volume_search returned three digitized volumes for the coal region, 1870-1900: Mine Worker Employment Cards (imageGroupNumber 002240015, Schuylkill, 1870-1900, 410 images, 95% record-searchable, full-text searchable); Mine Accident Reports (002240016, Luzerne, 1870-1895, 287 images, 0% record-searchable, not full-text searchable -- browse-only); Colliery Payroll Ledgers (002240017, Lackawanna, 1878-1900, 199 images, 0% record-searchable, not full-text searchable -- browse-only). totalResults for the search was 23 with a nextPageToken (PA_COAL_REGION_PAGE_2) -- only 3 of 23 matching volumes were detailed above; the rest were not examined in this survey.
