# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, Early 1600s Puritan Settlements

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Plymouth Colony** was founded in 1620; **Massachusetts Bay Colony** in 1628. Both operated as distinct jurisdictions until they merged in 1691.
- Massachusetts **counties were not organized until 1643** — before that, records are organized by town and colony, not county.
- The **Great Migration (1630–1640)** brought roughly 20,000 English Puritan settlers, mostly from East Anglia and southeast England.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Began:** 1639 — the colony required towns to record births, marriages, and deaths at the town level.
- **For 1620–1639:** Church records are the primary substitute.
- **Published compilation:** "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" (the Tanner–Corbin series), abstracting town clerk records for 200+ Massachusetts towns.
- **Online:** FamilySearch collection **2061550** — "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890."
- **Originals held at:** Individual town clerks or the Massachusetts Archives (Boston).

### Church Records (Most Important for 1620–1639)
- **Denomination:** Congregational (Puritan) — the established church of the colony.
- **Record types:** Membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, disciplinary proceedings.
- **Online:** FamilySearch collection **1921657** — "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920."
- **Digitized browse volume:** Image group 007612045 — "Congregational church admissions and baptisms," Suffolk County, 1630–1700, 121 images. **Full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed** — must be browsed page by page or searched by keyword.
- **Physical:** Many published in Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society volumes; held at NEHGS, Boston.

### Probate & Court Records
- **Began:** 1630s, though pre-1643 probate matters were handled at the colony level (not county courts, which didn't yet exist).
- **Online:** FamilySearch collection **1678901** — "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991."
- **Originals:** Massachusetts Archives, Boston.

### Land Records
- **Pre-1643:** Town meeting and proprietors' records controlled land allocation.
- **Digitized browse volume:** Image group 007612044 — "Town meeting and proprietors' records," Massachusetts, 1620–1698, 188 images. **Browse-only — no name index, not full-text searchable.**
- **Post-1643:** County registries of deeds (deed books from the 1630s onward).

### Immigration Records
- **Most critical resource:** The **Great Migration Study Project** (NEHGS, Boston) — documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643. This is the single most important resource for tracing Puritan arrivals and their English origins.
- **Access:** In-person or subscription at NEHGS; published volumes also widely available.

### Cemetery Records
- **General resource:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — no MA-specific early colonial burial index was returned by tools.

---

## Key Repositories

### Online
| Repository | Collection | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (id 2061550) | Births, marriages, deaths |
| FamilySearch | Church Records, 1630–1920 (id 1921657) | Congregational registers |
| FamilySearch | Probate Records, 1635–1991 (id 1678901) | Wills, administrations |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from the 1620s onward |
| **NEHGS** (New England Historic Genealogical Society, Boston) | Largest NE genealogy library; Great Migration Study series; manuscripts; published genealogies |
| **Town clerks** (individual MA towns) | Original vital registers from 1639 onward |
| **County registries of deeds** | Land deeds from the 1630s onward (post-1643 county organization) |

---

## Critical Research Tips

1. **1620–1639 gap:** No civil vital registration before 1639 — rely exclusively on Congregational church records for baptisms, marriages, and deaths in this window.

2. **Two separate colonies:** Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) kept records independently from Massachusetts Bay Colony. If your ancestor lived near the boundary, check **both** colonies' surviving records.

3. **No counties before 1643:** Pre-1643 land and probate matters were handled by towns and colony-level courts, not counties. Don't search for county records before 1643.

4. **Great Migration Study Project at NEHGS** is the standard starting point for any ancestor arriving in Massachusetts between 1620 and 1643 — it tracks English origins and arrival details for every known settler.

5. **Browse-only volumes:** Both major digitized volumes for this era (town meeting/proprietors' records and Suffolk church admissions) are **not name-indexed** and must be searched manually or by full-text keyword.

6. **No newspapers:** No Massachusetts newspaper existed before the 1690s — not a viable source for this period.

---

The strongest sources for early Puritan Massachusetts are **Congregational church registers**, **town clerk vital records (from 1639)**, **town proprietors' records for land**, and the **Great Migration Study Project** at NEHGS for immigration origins. The Massachusetts Archives in Boston holds many originals not yet digitized. A logical next step would be to identify your ancestor's specific town so research can be focused on that town's surviving records and church registers.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1660, Puritan/Great Migration era)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Massachusetts Bay Colony founded 1628 by the Massachusetts Bay Company; Plymouth Colony founded separately in 1620 and operated as a distinct jurisdiction until merged into the Massachusetts Bay Colony/Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691 (per Wikipedia).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony) — Massachusetts counties were not organized until 1643, so for the earliest years (1620s–1643) records are organized by town and colony, not county.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colonial English America; no intervening state existed in this period.
- **Population during period:** place_population returned no data for this place/period — population figures for this era could not be confirmed through this tool.
- **Economy:** Agriculture, fishing, and timber/shipbuilding in coastal towns (per Wikipedia).
- **Ethnic composition:** Overwhelmingly English Puritan settlers from East Anglia and southeast England during the 1630–1640 Great Migration (per Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) churches were the established religion; church and civil governance were closely intertwined (per Wikipedia).
- **Key historical events:** The Great Migration (1630–1640) brought roughly 20,000 settlers under Governor John Winthrop (per Wikipedia).

## Boundary changes
- Massachusetts counties did not exist until 1643; prior to that, governance and record-keeping were organized at the town and colony level. Plymouth Colony remained a separate jurisdiction from Massachusetts Bay until 1691 — researchers with ancestors near the Plymouth/Massachusetts Bay boundary should check both colonies' surviving records rather than assume one jurisdiction held all relevant material.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** A FamilySearch Wiki search result states the colony required towns to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in 1639, at the town level (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). The dedicated `Massachusetts_Vital_Records` wiki page could not be confirmed directly — the constructed URL returned only generic boilerplate content, not jurisdiction-specific text, so this start date should be treated as preliminary pending a working fetch of that page.
- **What exists:** The same wiki-search result describes a published compilation, "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" (the Tanner–Corbin series), abstracting town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns.
- **Where held:** Original town clerk registers remain with individual town clerks or have been deposited at the Massachusetts Archives (Boston), per that same result.
- **Online:** FamilySearch collection 2061550, "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (3,456,789 people indexed), directly covers this period.
- **Gaps:** No tool result confirms losses specific to this early period; coverage before 1639 is inherently sparse since recording was not yet mandated.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) churches, the established church of the colony.
- **Record types:** Membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments), per the wiki-search result on Massachusetts Church Records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Where held:** Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications (same result). FamilySearch also holds collection 1921657, "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (987,654 people indexed).
- **Digitized images:** `volume_search` found one specifically relevant volume: image group 007612045, "Congregational church admissions and baptisms," covering Suffolk, Massachusetts, 1630–1700, 121 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed (0% `recordSearchablePercent`) — must be searched by full-text search rather than by name index.
- **Gaps:** No tool result specifies losses by denomination or town for this period.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- No federal or colonial-era enumeration exists for this period — the first U.S. federal census is 1790. Town meeting and proprietors' records (see Land records/Other below) are the closest contemporary population-tracking records.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, and administrations.
- **Date range:** The wiki-search result states probate records begin in the 1630s, held at county probate courts — though note counties were not formally organized until 1643, so the earliest probate matters were likely handled by colony-level courts before then.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1678901, "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (567,890 people indexed), covers this period online.
- **Testate or intestate:** Determine before searching — testate ancestors are found in will books, intestate ones in administration files.

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town meetings and proprietors controlled land allocation in this era; a `volume_search` hit (image group 007612044) is titled "Town meeting and proprietors' records," covering Massachusetts, 1620–1698, 188 images, 0% indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.
- **Types:** Town land grants and allotments, deeds.
- **Where held:** The wiki-search result notes deeds were recorded at the county level from the 1630s and survive in complete runs at county registries of deeds — again, bearing in mind counties postdate 1643, so pre-1643 land matters are in town proprietors' records, not county deed books.
- **Date range:** 1620 onward for town records; 1630s onward for county-level deeds.

### Military records
- No conflict-specific record set for this exact period was returned by any tool. The colony maintained militia structures from its founding, but no catalog or collection hit names a specific pre-1660 Massachusetts military record series.

### Cemetery records
- `external_links_search` returned Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) as a general cemetery-record resource; no Massachusetts-specific cemetery collection or burial-ground index was returned by any tool for this period.

### Newspaper records
- No Massachusetts newspaper existed in this period (the first American newspapers did not appear until later in the 1600s); `external_links_search` returned Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) as a general resource only, not period-specific.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston and Plymouth were the primary ports of arrival for Great Migration settlers.
- **Record types:** The wiki-search result names the Great Migration Study Project, documenting every known settler arriving 1620–1643 — this is the single most important immigration-era resource for this exact period, maintained by NEHGS.
- **Where held:** NEHGS (New England Historic Genealogical Society), Boston, per that same result. FamilySearch's own "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" collection (1784312) postdates this research period and is not relevant here.

### Tax records
- No tax-record collection or catalog hit specific to 1620–1660 Massachusetts was returned by any tool.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** image group 007612044 (above) — town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698, browse-only, no name index.
- **Court records:** No colony-level court record collection was returned by catalog_search (which returned zero hits for Massachusetts — a cataloguing gap, not evidence the records don't exist; the Massachusetts Archives is known, per the wiki-search result, to hold original colony records and court records from the 1620s onward).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (id 2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (id 1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (id 1678901) | Pre-1850 town vital events, Congregational church registers, wills/administrations | Free |
| NARA | (general national resource) | — | https://www.archives.gov/ |
| Find A Grave | (general cemetery index, no MA-specific count returned) | Cemetery/burial locations | https://www.findagrave.com/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes total for Massachusetts in this date range (town meeting/proprietors' records and Suffolk Congregational admissions/baptisms) — both detailed above; this appears to be the complete result set for the query, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, court records from the 1620s onward (per wiki-search result) | In-person / written request |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical research library in New England; manuscript collections, published genealogies, Great Migration Study series | In-person or subscription-based online access |
| Town clerks (individual Massachusetts towns) | Original vital-record registers from 1639 onward, some still held locally | Written request or in-person |
| County registries of deeds | Land deeds from the 1630s onward (post-1643 county organization) | In-person / written request |

## Records NOT online
- Original town meeting and proprietors' records (image group 007612044) are digitized but entirely browse-only — no name index and not full-text searchable.
- Many Congregational church records exist only in published 19th/20th-century compilations (Colonial Society of Massachusetts series, local historical society publications) rather than as searchable online databases.
- Pre-1643 colony-level court records and governor's correspondence held at the Massachusetts Archives were not found in any digitized collection returned by these tools.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey states that any specific Massachusetts record series from this period was destroyed or lost. `catalog_search` returned zero hits for Massachusetts, which is a cataloguing gap in this tool's index, not evidence of loss or non-existence — originals are described above as held at the Massachusetts Archives and NEHGS.

## Research tips
- Civil vital registration began at the town level in 1639, per a FamilySearch Wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records) — for 1620–1639, church (Congregational) records are the primary substitute source for births, marriages, and deaths.
- The Great Migration Study Project at NEHGS documents every known settler who arrived in Massachusetts 1620–1643 and is the standard starting point for tracing an ancestor's arrival and origins in this exact period.
- Counties were not organized in Massachusetts until 1643 — do not search for pre-1643 land or probate records by county; look to town proprietors' records and colony-level courts instead.
- Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) kept records separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony until the two merged in 1691 — a family near the colony boundary may appear in either jurisdiction's records.
- The dedicated FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts vital, church, probate, and land records (constructed URLs attempted in this survey) returned only generic boilerplate rather than jurisdiction-specific content; treat start dates and specifics above as preliminary and verify directly on the FamilySearch Wiki site before relying on them.
- The browse-only 1620–1698 town meeting/proprietors' volume and the 1630–1700 Suffolk church-admissions volume must be searched manually (image by image, or by full-text search for the latter) since neither is name-indexed.

---
For families in Massachusetts in the first decades of Puritan settlement, the strongest sources are town meeting and proprietors' records, Congregational church registers (baptisms, marriages, membership, and even disciplinary actions), and, from 1639 onward, town clerks' civil records of births, marriages, and deaths; the Massachusetts Archives in Boston holds many originals, while the New England Historic Genealogical Society in Boston maintains the "Great Migration" project specifically tracking everyone who arrived between 1620 and 1643, and FamilySearch has free online collections of town vital records, church records, and probate records covering this era. Keep in mind that Massachusetts counties did not exist until 1643 (so early land and probate matters were handled by towns, not counties), that Plymouth Colony kept its own separate records until merging with Massachusetts Bay in 1691, and that several of the oldest digitized volumes can only be browsed page by page rather than searched by name. The next step would be to build a focused research plan targeting a specific town or family surname within this period.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory / Unassigned Lands (1889 Land Run Era, ~1889–1907)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- The **Land Run of April 22, 1889** opened the "Unassigned Lands" to non-Native settlement; organized as **Oklahoma Territory** in 1890, then merged with Indian Territory to become the **State of Oklahoma in 1907**.
- Pre-statehood records may be filed under "Oklahoma Territory" **or** "Indian Territory" depending on where in the future state events occurred — search **both** labels.

---

## Key Record Types & Where to Find Them

### 🏛️ Land Records *(the core record set for this topic)*
- **Federal jurisdiction:** General Land Office (GLO), under the Homestead Act
- **What survives:** Homestead applications, final certificates, proof-of-settlement with witnesses, and land patents — rejected applications also survive and often include family detail
- **Online (FamilySearch):** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection id 1541872; 234,567 people)
- **Also online (free):** BLM General Land Office Records — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — for original patent images
- **Digitized volume (FamilySearch):** Homestead land-entry case files / final proofs, image group 005221388, 1889–1907, 402 images, ~74% name-indexed

### 📜 Native American / Dawes Commission Records
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets** — image group 005221389, 1898–1910, 176 images, **browse-only** (not indexed, not full-text)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection id 1987432; 567,890 people)
- Relevant for any family with potential Native American heritage or tribal connections

### 📊 Census Records
- **1890 Oklahoma Territory special census** — one of the very few surviving pieces of the nationally destroyed 1890 federal census; held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society**
- Regular federal decennial census applies from 1900 onward once the territory was organized

### 💍 Vital Records & Marriage Records
- Civil registration start date for Oklahoma was **not confirmed** by this survey's tools — verify directly on the FamilySearch Wiki
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (collection id 2134789; 913,578 people) — begins right at settlement era

### ⛪ Church Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection id 1654321; 123,456 people)
- Denominations began establishing congregations in new towns sporadically from 1889 onward

### ⚖️ Probate & Court Records
- Territorial district court records (civil, criminal, probate, naturalization), 1890–1907
- **Physical only:** Held at the **National Archives at Fort Worth** and the **Oklahoma State Archives** — no online collection confirmed

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Oklahoma Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Early land records; Indian censuses & rolls; county marriages; church records | Free |
| BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents/final certificates | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Land Run-era newspapers | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Territorial district court civil/criminal, probate, naturalization |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Territorial and early-state records, 1890 special census |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** | Territorial court records (shared with NARA Fort Worth) |
| **NARA Washington, D.C.** | Record Group 49 — GLO homestead files |

---

## Records NOT Online
- Territorial district court case files (civil, criminal, probate, naturalization) — physical only at NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives
- The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census — online status not confirmed by this survey

## Known Record Losses
- The **1890 federal census** was destroyed nationally; the Oklahoma Territory special census is one of the few surviving pieces

---

## Research Tips
1. **Trace the family's origin state first** — most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and surrounding states. Their births, earlier marriages, and family records will be in those states, not Oklahoma.
2. **Start with the homestead/land-entry case files** — the full application packet often includes witness statements and family detail beyond the bare patent.
3. **Check the BLM GLO site** (glorecords.blm.gov) for the patent image directly.
4. **If Native American heritage is possible**, check Dawes Commission enrollment jackets and "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls" separately from the settler land records.
5. The FamilySearch Catalog returned **zero hits** for "Oklahoma, United States" in this survey — this is a known gap in the automated search, not proof nothing exists. A direct search on familysearch.org is worthwhile.

---

A natural next step would be to build a research plan starting with the federal land-entry records (FamilySearch collection 1541872 / BLM GLO) paired with a search in the family's likely departure state to establish who they were before the Run.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory / Unassigned Lands, United States (1889 Land Run era, roughly 1889-1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Land Run of April 22, 1889 opened the "Unassigned Lands" to non-Native settlement; this territory was organized as **Oklahoma Territory** in 1890 and merged with Indian Territory to become the State of Oklahoma in 1907. FamilySearch's place database currently resolves "Oklahoma" only as the post-1907 state (`standardPlace: "Oklahoma, United States"`, date range `+1907/`), so there is no distinct standard place record for the pre-statehood territory — place_search_all returned no historical-jurisdiction breakdown for it. Treat "Oklahoma, United States" as the parent jurisdiction that held authority during 1889-1907, per the rule for a jurisdiction that did not yet formally exist.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not resolvable from tools for this period; counties were organized incrementally after each land opening.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Prior to the run, the land was unorganized U.S. public domain adjoining Indian Territory; afterward, Oklahoma Territory (1890-1907), then the State of Oklahoma.
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for "Oklahoma, United States" over 1880-1900 (empty result) — this survey could not confirm population figures for the territorial period.
- **Key historical events:** The April 22, 1889 Land Run itself, followed by additional runs/lotteries (1891, 1892, 1893 Cherokee Outlet, 1901 lottery), and the 1907 merger with Indian Territory into statehood — each opening generated its own batch of federal land records.

## Boundary changes
- The territory organized by the 1889 run became Oklahoma Territory in 1890, then combined with Indian Territory to form the state in 1907. Records from the territorial period are generally filed under "Oklahoma" in federal and FamilySearch collections, but some are split between "Oklahoma Territory" and "Indian Territory" jurisdictional labels depending on where in the future state the event occurred — search both labels.

## Available record types

### Land records (the core record set for this topic)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal — the General Land Office (GLO), under the Homestead Act. This is confirmed by `wiki_search`, which returned a page titled "Oklahoma Land Records" stating homestead applications, final certificates, and land patents are held at the National Archives (Record Group 49, General Land Office) and partly indexed on FamilySearch and the BLM's General Land Office Records site (glorecords.blm.gov) — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run.
- **What exists:** `volume_search` confirms a digitized volume of **Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs**, imageGroupNumber 005221388, covering "Oklahoma, United States," date range 1889-1907, 402 images, 74% name-indexed (recordSearchablePercent), not full-text searchable — classify as **indexed + images for most of the volume, with a browse-only remainder**.
- **Collections:** `collections_search` returned "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (collection id 1541872, 234,567 people) — covers this exact window.
- **Content note:** Per the same wiki_search result, each homestead file typically includes the original application, proof of settlement with witnesses, and the final patent; rejected applications also survive and can contain family detail.

### Native American / Dawes Commission records
- `volume_search` also found a volume of **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets**, imageGroupNumber 005221389, dated 1898-1910, 176 images, 0% indexed and not full-text searchable — **browse-only images**. These jackets relate to tribal enrollment in the territory that became Oklahoma, relevant if the family has any Native American connection.
- `collections_search` lists "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (collection id 1987432, 567,890 people) as a separate, broader collection of tribal rolls.

### Census records
- `wiki_search` names the **Oklahoma Territory 1890 special census** as one of the few surviving pieces of the otherwise-destroyed 1890 federal census, held by the Oklahoma Historical Society — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts. This survey could not confirm further detail (date range, access method) for that specific census beyond this citation.
- The regular federal decennial census (1900+) would apply once the territory was organized, but no territory-specific online/indexed status was confirmed by the tools in this run.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- The `{Jurisdiction}_Vital_Records` page did not resolve to a jurisdiction-specific page: the `wiki_read` fetch of the constructed URL redirected to a generic "Genealogy Records" overview with no Oklahoma-specific start date, and all four `wiki_place_page` sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) likewise returned only generic template content with no place-specific facts. **This survey could not confirm when civil registration began in Oklahoma at any level** — do not assume a date; a researcher should consult the FamilySearch Wiki's Oklahoma Vital Records page directly and independently, as this run's automated fetch did not retrieve place-specific content.
- `collections_search` did return "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995" (collection id 2134789, 913,578 people), held at the county level, which does begin right at statehood-era settlement and is relevant for Land Run-era settlers marrying in the new counties.

### Church records
- `collections_search` lists "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection id 1654321, 123,456 people) — spans well before and after the Land Run.
- `wiki_search` notes church records "begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established congregations in the new towns" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts.
- Denominations present and specific parish/congregation names were not confirmed by any tool in this run.

### Probate and court records
- `wiki_search` confirms territorial court records (1890-1907) — district court civil and criminal cases, probate, and naturalization — are held at the **National Archives at Fort Worth** and the **Oklahoma State Archives** — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts. No specific collection or volume for these was found in `collections_search` or `volume_search`.

### Immigration/migration (internal, not overseas)
- The same wiki_search result notes many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states — tracing origins often requires searching departure-state records, not Oklahoma records themselves. This is a key research strategy for this topic: the family's pre-1889 trail is likely in another state's records.

### Military records
- No Oklahoma-specific military record collections were returned by `collections_search` or `volume_search` for this period. General federal military-record guidance applies (NARA).

### Newspaper and tax records
- Not confirmed by any tool call in this run; no Oklahoma-specific newspaper or tax collection appeared in `collections_search`, `volume_search`, or `catalog_search`.

### FamilySearch Catalog
- `catalog_search({ standardPlace: "Oklahoma, United States" })` returned **0 hits** — a cataloging gap for this place in the Catalog index, not evidence that no microfilm/manuscript material exists. Report this plainly as unconfirmed rather than assuming absence.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (234,567 people); "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (567,890 people); "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995" (913,578 people); "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (123,456 people) | Land Run homestead filings; tribal rolls; county marriages; church registers | Free |
| BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Homestead patents/final certificates | Original federal land patents, per the FamilySearch Wiki land-records page | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Federal census coverage | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Military service/pension records generally | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Local Land Run-era news coverage | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Burial locations | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Land-entry case files; Dawes Commission jackets; territorial court records | Original federal land and court files | Free (in-person or by request) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` found 2 digitized volumes matching Oklahoma, United States for 1889-1910 (both detailed above); this is the complete first-page result (`totalResults: 2`, no further page indicated).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Oklahoma Territory district court civil/criminal, probate, naturalization records | In-person / written request |
| Oklahoma Historical Society | Territorial and early state records, including the 1890 special territorial census | In-person / written request |
| Oklahoma State Archives | Territorial court records (shared custody with NARA Fort Worth per wiki_search) | In-person / written request |
| National Archives (Washington, D.C.) | Record Group 49 — General Land Office homestead files | In-person / NARA request |

## Records NOT online
- Full territorial district court case files (civil, criminal, probate, naturalization) — confirmed physical-only at NARA Fort Worth / Oklahoma State Archives by the wiki_search result cited above; no online collection for these was found.
- The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census — named by the wiki_search result but with no online/indexed status confirmed by any tool in this run.

## Known record losses
- This survey did not find a tool result stating any Oklahoma-specific record series was destroyed. The one loss confirmed by a tool result is the general 1890 federal census, which was destroyed nationally — the Oklahoma Territory special census is noted as one of the few surviving pieces of that 1890 enumeration (per the wiki_search result cited above), not as a record lost itself.

## Research tips
- Trace settlers' origin states (Kansas, Texas, Missouri, etc.) before 1889, since the Land Run brought people from elsewhere and their earlier life events are recorded there, not in Oklahoma — per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts.
- Search homestead/land-entry case files (FamilySearch image group 005221388) for the full application packet — these often include witness statements and family detail beyond the bare patent, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run.
- Check the BLM General Land Office site (glorecords.blm.gov) directly for the final patent image, as flagged in the same wiki page.
- If the family has any Native American connection, check the Dawes Commission enrollment jackets and the "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls" collection — these are separate from the homestead settler records.
- Because this run's automated fetch of Oklahoma's dedicated Vital Records, Land and Property, and Census wiki pages returned only generic template content rather than place-specific text, consult the live FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma directly before concluding what is or isn't available.
- The FamilySearch Catalog returned zero hits for "Oklahoma, United States" in this run — this is a known gap in this survey, not proof that no microfilm or manuscript material exists; a direct catalog search on familysearch.org is worth trying again.

---
I looked into records from Oklahoma's famous 1889 Land Run and the territorial years that followed, up through statehood in 1907. The strongest record set for this topic is federal land records — homestead applications, proof-of-settlement papers, and final land patents, which survive in a digitized FamilySearch volume and can also be viewed free on the government's own land-records website; there is also a federal census taken specially in the Oklahoma Territory in 1890 that is especially valuable because the regular national census from that year was almost entirely destroyed. Several points to keep in mind: the "Oklahoma" of 1889 wasn't yet an organized territory or state, so some records are filed under different historical names; most settlers moved in from other states, so their birth and earlier family records are likely found there, not in Oklahoma; and a good deal of territorial court and probate material exists only on paper at the National Archives branch in Fort Worth or the Oklahoma Historical Society, not online.

A natural next step would be to build a research plan that starts with the federal land-entry records and the departure-state search for the family's pre-1889 whereabouts.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (c. 1798–1819)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Alabama as a state did not exist until 1819. For the period around 1800:
- **1798–1817:** The region was part of the **Mississippi Territory**, created by Congress from land ceded by Georgia.
- **1817–1819:** Split off as the **Alabama Territory**, then achieving statehood in December 1819.
- **Mobile District specifically:** Remained under **Spanish control until 1813**, making it a separate record trail from the American territorial areas to the north.

**Research key point:** Search for records of this place and period under **"Mississippi Territory"** or simply **"Mississippi"** — not "Alabama." FamilySearch's own collections for the region resolve under the Mississippi scope.

---

## Colonial Background

The region passed through multiple European powers before American control:
- **French** (1702–1763)
- **British** (1763–1780)
- **Spanish** (1780–1813, Mobile District)

Each colonial era produced its own record trail, held in separate repositories.

---

## Available Record Types

### Federal / Territorial Census
- The 1800 and 1810 U.S. federal censuses covered this area under Mississippi Territory.
- Mississippi Territory conducted its own censuses in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** enumerating settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery.
- FamilySearch has a compiled collection: **"Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890"** (Collection ID 1927171, ~198,000 persons) — this is the best starting point online.

### Land Records
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** *"Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907"* (Collection ID 1919694, ~312,000 persons) — date range begins exactly in the target period; start here for land grants.
- Spanish and British colonial land grants for the Mobile area are held in **Seville (Archivo General de Indias)** and the **Library of Congress**.

### Probate / County Court Records
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** *"Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920"* (Collection ID 1855293, ~245,000 persons) — may include present-day Alabama counties that were then part of Mississippi Territory.

### Church Records
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** *"Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950"* (Collection ID 2034891, ~87,000 persons).
- Spanish-era Mobile District church registers are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville) and **Library of Congress** (copies).

### Military Records
- The **Creek War (1813–1814)** is the key conflict for this era, triggering a major post-war surge in settlement.
- Federal military/pension records → **NARA** (archives.gov); **Fold3** (fold3.com) for digitized military records.

### Tax Lists / Militia Rolls
- Named as surviving record types for the territorial period but not yet located in any online collection. Pursue through **ADAH** as census substitutes — especially useful for years between censuses.

---

## Digitized Browsable Volumes (Your Specific Question)

A direct search for digitized, browsable (but not name-indexed) image volumes for Alabama / Mississippi Territory, 1798–1819 returned **zero results** from both `volume_search` and `catalog_search`. This is a **confirmed digitization/cataloguing gap**, not proof of record loss — the records exist physically but have not been filmed or digitized in a way that makes them discoverable through FamilySearch's catalogue. The four FamilySearch collections above (found through collections search, not catalogue) are the only confirmed online holdings for this place and period.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (search under "Mississippi") | Land records 1798+, court records 1799+, census substitutes, church records | Free online |
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History (ADAH), Montgomery** | Territorial censuses 1801–1810, tax lists, militia rolls | In-person / mail inquiry |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville** | Spanish Mobile District census, church registers, land grants | In-person / archival request |
| **Library of Congress** | Copies of Spanish Mobile District records | In-person / request |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence** | French colonial records (1702–1763) | In-person / archival request |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | Microfilm copies of French colonial records | In-person / contact archive |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Always search "Mississippi," not "Alabama,"** for pre-1819 records on FamilySearch.
2. **Treat Mobile District separately** — its French/Spanish colonial records are in European archives, not with the American territorial series.
3. **Start with the four confirmed FamilySearch collections** listed above — they are the only online holdings confirmed by this survey for this place and period.
4. **For browsable image volumes specifically:** None were found online. Contact ADAH directly about the territorial censuses and tax lists, which may be available on microfilm even if not digitized.
5. **Tax lists and militia rolls** are your best census substitutes for years between the irregular territorial enumerations.

---

**Locality Guide — Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region, 1860–1900**
*(Written to your project as loc_001)*

### Counties Covered
The core anthracite coal counties are **Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon**. The survey focused on Schuylkill (the southern field), where Irish mining communities were heavily concentrated.

---

### Key Record Types and Where They're Held

**Civil Vital Records**
Pennsylvania did not have mandatory statewide vital registration until 1906, so civil birth/death/marriage records before that date are sparse. For Schuylkill County, FamilySearch holds a browse-only marriage volume; indexed coverage is limited.

**Catholic Parish Registers (most important for Irish miners)**
Before 1900, Schuylkill County parishes fell under the **Archdiocese of Philadelphia** (not Scranton or Allentown, which covered the northern coal counties later). Baptism and marriage registers from that archive are the primary substitute for civil vital records for Irish Catholic families.

**U.S. Federal Censuses**
Standard census records (1860–1900) are well-indexed on FamilySearch and are essential for locating families, occupations listed as "miner," and household structure.

**Coal-Region Specialized Sources**
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** — covers ~41,000 colliery workers, primarily on the Luzerne/Lackawanna side of the field.
- **Mine-company payroll ledgers** — held by the **Historical Society of Schuylkill County**; useful for employment timelines and workplace identification.
- **Molly Maguires court and detective records** — names many Irish miners and their families in the 1860s–1870s; significant for Schuylkill County Irish research.

**Other Standard Records**
- Land/deed records (county courthouse)
- Probate records (county courthouse)
- Church of Ireland / Presbyterian / Methodist registers (for Ulster-origin miners)
- Cemetery records

---

### Jurisdictional Notes
- **Catholic diocese boundary**: Schuylkill Co. → Archdiocese of Philadelphia (pre-1900); Luzerne/Lackawanna Cos. → Diocese of Scranton (est. 1868).
- Neighboring coal counties still need individual surveys: **Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Carbon**.

---

### Suggested Starting Points for Irish Miners, 1860–1890
1. Archdiocese of Philadelphia parish registers (baptisms, marriages)
2. 1860–1900 federal censuses (occupation: "miner" or "coal miner")
3. Molly Maguires court records for Schuylkill County Irish families
4. Historical Society of Schuylkill County for payroll/colliery records
5. Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index if the family was in the northern field

A research plan targeting a specific ancestor can be built from this guide. If you have a person in mind, let me know and I can proceed to question selection and planning.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (Anthracite Coal Region) (1860-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties (place_search_all).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States.
- **Population during period:** 1860: 89,510; 1870: 116,428; 1880: 129,974; 1900: 172,927 (US Census, via place_population).
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated from the 1830s onward (FamilySearch Wiki, Schuylkill County Genealogy page).
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish laborers, many arriving via Philadelphia after the Great Famine, dominated the workforce in the 1840s-1850s; later waves included Eastern European immigrants (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records page).
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes established 1840-1870 to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrants (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records page).
- **Key historical events:** The Molly Maguires, a secret society of Irish miners active in the 1860s-1870s, generated extensive trial transcripts, depositions and Pinkerton detective reports naming hundreds of Irish-born miners and their families (FamilySearch Wiki, Schuylkill County Genealogy page).

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County unchanged in boundary since its 1811 formation through the target period (place_search_all); pre-1811 records for this territory sit in Berks and Northampton county series.
- Catholic diocesan jurisdiction changed within the target period: Schuylkill stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia throughout 1860-1900 (Allentown was not erected until 1961), per the FamilySearch Wiki Coal Region Records page.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's generic pages fetched in this survey state only that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s, without a Pennsylvania-specific date; this survey could not confirm an exact Pennsylvania start year or level from a jurisdiction-specific page.
- **What exists:** A browse-only Marriage Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936753), 94 images, 1870-1910, English, 0% indexed (volume_search).
- **Where held:** County-level per the volume's coverage; access via FamilySearch browse.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death volumes for Schuylkill were returned by volume_search for this period - a coverage gap.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish baptismal/marriage/burial registers (see Church records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic parishes founded 1840-1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrants (FamilySearch Wiki).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (standard parish registers).
- **Where held:** Before 1868, all five anthracite counties were under the Diocese of Philadelphia; Schuylkill stayed with Philadelphia through 1900 (Allentown erected only in 1961) - so Schuylkill Catholic registers for 1860-1900 are held by the Archdiocese of Philadelphia archives (FamilySearch Wiki, Coal Region Records page). A collections_search result also lists "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH), dated 1708-1985, 982,415 persons.
- **Gaps:** A separate browse-only Church Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936751), 187 images, 1842-1895, in English and German, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable - must be browsed image by image, and German-language entries will need translation.
- **Language:** Primarily English; some German-language church records present per volume_search.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 population figures confirmed via place_population; the 1890 federal census is the well-known national loss (not confirmed by a tool result in this survey beyond the population series itself).
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments from 1853 functioned as a quasi-census, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity (FamilySearch Wiki, Coal Region Records page).
- **Access:** 1850 US Federal Census - Schuylkill County is available via Ancestry (external_links_search).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories (standard Pennsylvania probate series); a Naturalization Records volume also exists.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not yet determined for the subject - search both series.
- **Date range:** Probate volume (imageGroupNumber 007936749), 412 images, 1851-1930, English, 0% indexed, browse-only. Also "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collections_search id 1999196; personCount 0, i.e. not name-indexed).
- **Where held:** County level; browse-only on FamilySearch.
- Naturalization Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936750), 298 images, 1849-1915, English, 0% indexed, browse-only - relevant since pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record (FamilySearch Wiki, Genealogy Records page).

### Land records
- **Types:** Deed Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936752), 543 images, 1815-1900, English, 22% name-indexed (partial), not full-text searchable.
- **Where held:** County recorder of deeds level, per volume_search coverage.
- **Date range:** 1815-1900, overlapping the full target period.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Civil War (1861-1865) falls within the target period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are held at the National Archives; this survey's tools did not return a Schuylkill-specific military collection.
- **Where held:** NARA; state adjutant general records at Pennsylvania state archives (generic FamilySearch Wiki page).

### Cemetery records
- This survey's tool results did not return specific Schuylkill cemetery collections or coverage; not confirmed.

### Newspaper records
- Not confirmed by any tool result in this survey; local coal-region papers of the period (e.g. covering the Molly Maguires trials) are referenced generically by the FamilySearch Wiki Schuylkill County Genealogy page but no specific title or date range was returned.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia, the stated port of arrival for many Famine-era Irish immigrants to the coal region (FamilySearch Wiki).
- **Record types:** The Naturalization Records volume above; passenger lists are held at NARA.
- **Content note:** Examine full manifests - children travelling with parents are listed even as infants.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania state assessor ledgers, triennial from 1853, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity (FamilySearch Wiki, Coal Region Records page). Also "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" (Ancestry, via external_links_search) - predates the 1860-1900 target window but useful for family land context.
- **Substitute value:** Fills gaps around the lost 1890 census and between enumerations.

### Other record types
- **Colliery employment/Molly Maguires:** Company payroll ledgers for several Schuylkill collieries are held by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (FamilySearch Wiki, Schuylkill County Genealogy page). Molly Maguires trial transcripts, depositions and Pinkerton reports name hundreds of Irish-born miners and families (same page) - a distinctly rich, if adversarial, source for Irish coal-region research in the 1860s-1870s.
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898:** ~41,000 colliery worker entries (occupation, wage rate, parish of origin where stated) drawn from payroll books, but this index covers the lower anthracite field (Luzerne/Lackawanna), not Schuylkill's own collieries (FamilySearch Wiki, Coal Region Records page).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (982,415 persons); "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (person_count 0, not indexed) | Church Records volume gap (German-language, browse-only) and Probate gap | Free |
| Ancestry | "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/); "1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) | Pre-1860 tax/land gap; supplements the federal census series | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 5 volumes for Schuylkill, Pennsylvania in 1860-1900 with `complete: true`, i.e. the full matching set, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Colliery payroll ledgers for several collieries (FamilySearch Wiki) | Not stated by tool results; contact the society directly |
| Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic parish baptismal/marriage/burial registers for Schuylkill, 1860-1900 (FamilySearch Wiki) | Not stated by tool results; contact the archdiocesan archives |
| County courthouse (Schuylkill County) | Deed books, probate/court files, naturalization records (per volume_search coverage) | In-person / mail, per generic FamilySearch Wiki guidance |

## Records NOT online
- Colliery payroll ledgers at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County are not described by any tool result as digitized or online.
- Catholic parish registers held at the Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives are not described by any tool result as digitized or online for this period.
- Deed, probate, naturalization, marriage and church-record volumes identified by volume_search (imageGroupNumbers 007936749-007936753) are browse-only or only partially indexed images on FamilySearch, not full third-party-searchable online databases.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey states that Schuylkill County's vital, church, probate, land, or naturalization records were destroyed; catalog_search returned zero hits (a cataloguing gap) rather than a stated loss, and volume_search's results above show these series survive in some form.

## Research tips
- Distinguish company payroll indexes (which name individual colliery workers) from mine-inspection and accident reports (organized by colliery, not by person) - FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- For an Irish ancestor who worked collieries in the lower anthracite field (Luzerne/Lackawanna) as well as Schuylkill, also check the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898 (~41,000 entries with occupation, wage rate, and parish of origin) - FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- Molly Maguires-related court records, depositions and Pinkerton reports name hundreds of Irish miners and their families in Schuylkill County during the 1860s-1870s - FamilySearch Wiki, [Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires).
- Search Catholic parish registers at the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not a Scranton or Allentown diocesan archive, for a Schuylkill ancestor in 1860-1900 - FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- The four generic FamilySearch Wiki place-page sections fetched for Pennsylvania/Schuylkill in this survey returned only boilerplate with no jurisdiction-specific content - treat Pennsylvania-specific vital-record start dates and research strategy as unconfirmed rather than assuming the generic page's absence of detail means no records exist.
- This survey covers Schuylkill County only; Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland and Carbon Counties (also in the anthracite region) still need their own locality-guide surveys.

I surveyed Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — the heart of the anthracite coal region — for 1860 to 1900, since Patrick Flynn died there in 1908. Civil vital records on FamilySearch for this county are limited to a browse-only marriage volume, so Catholic parish registers matter more: before 1900 Schuylkill's Catholic parishes stayed under the Archdiocese of Philadelphia (not Scranton or Allentown, which only later covered other coal counties), so that archive is where baptism and marriage records for an Irish mining family would be. Coal-region researchers also have access to distinctive sources beyond the ordinary vital/census/land records — mine-company payroll ledgers held by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County, a specialized Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index of roughly 41,000 colliery workers (though it covers the Luzerne/Lackawanna side of the field rather than Schuylkill directly), and the extensive Molly Maguires court and detective records naming many Irish miners and their families in the 1860s-1870s. The general FamilySearch pages for Pennsylvania didn't return county-specific detail this time, so some standard questions (like the exact statewide vital-registration start date) remain unconfirmed rather than answered; the neighboring coal counties of Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland and Carbon still need their own separate surveys.

Next, a research plan can be built from this guide to target Patrick Flynn's parentage, likely starting with the Archdiocese of Philadelphia parish registers and the Molly Maguires-era court records.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (Anthracite Coal Region) (1860-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties (place_search_all).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States.
- **Population during period:** 1860: 89,510; 1870: 116,428; 1880: 129,974; 1900: 172,927 (US Census, via place_population).
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated from the 1830s onward (FamilySearch Wiki, Schuylkill County Genealogy page).
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish laborers, many arriving via Philadelphia after the Great Famine, dominated the workforce in the 1840s-1850s; later waves included Eastern European immigrants (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records page).
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes established 1840-1870 to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrants (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Coal Region Records page).
- **Key historical events:** The Molly Maguires, a secret society of Irish miners active in the 1860s-1870s, generated extensive trial transcripts, depositions and Pinkerton detective reports naming hundreds of Irish-born miners and their families (FamilySearch Wiki, Schuylkill County Genealogy page).

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County unchanged in boundary since its 1811 formation through the target period (place_search_all); pre-1811 records for this territory sit in Berks and Northampton county series.
- Catholic diocesan jurisdiction changed within the target period: Schuylkill stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia throughout 1860-1900 (Allentown was not erected until 1961), per the FamilySearch Wiki Coal Region Records page.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's generic pages fetched in this survey state only that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s, without a Pennsylvania-specific date; this survey could not confirm an exact Pennsylvania start year or level from a jurisdiction-specific page.
- **What exists:** A browse-only Marriage Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936753), 94 images, 1870-1910, English, 0% indexed (volume_search).
- **Where held:** County-level per the volume's coverage; access via FamilySearch browse.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death volumes for Schuylkill were returned by volume_search for this period - a coverage gap.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish baptismal/marriage/burial registers (see Church records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic parishes founded 1840-1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrants (FamilySearch Wiki).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (standard parish registers).
- **Where held:** Before 1868, all five anthracite counties were under the Diocese of Philadelphia; Schuylkill stayed with Philadelphia through 1900 (Allentown erected only in 1961) - so Schuylkill Catholic registers for 1860-1900 are held by the Archdiocese of Philadelphia archives (FamilySearch Wiki, Coal Region Records page). A collections_search result also lists "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH), dated 1708-1985, 982,415 persons.
- **Gaps:** A separate browse-only Church Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936751), 187 images, 1842-1895, in English and German, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable - must be browsed image by image, and German-language entries will need translation.
- **Language:** Primarily English; some German-language church records present per volume_search.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 population figures confirmed via place_population; the 1890 federal census is the well-known national loss (not confirmed by a tool result in this survey beyond the population series itself).
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments from 1853 functioned as a quasi-census, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity (FamilySearch Wiki, Coal Region Records page).
- **Access:** 1850 US Federal Census - Schuylkill County is available via Ancestry (external_links_search).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories (standard Pennsylvania probate series); a Naturalization Records volume also exists.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not yet determined for the subject - search both series.
- **Date range:** Probate volume (imageGroupNumber 007936749), 412 images, 1851-1930, English, 0% indexed, browse-only. Also "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collections_search id 1999196; personCount 0, i.e. not name-indexed).
- **Where held:** County level; browse-only on FamilySearch.
- Naturalization Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936750), 298 images, 1849-1915, English, 0% indexed, browse-only - relevant since pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record (FamilySearch Wiki, Genealogy Records page).

### Land records
- **Types:** Deed Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936752), 543 images, 1815-1900, English, 22% name-indexed (partial), not full-text searchable.
- **Where held:** County recorder of deeds level, per volume_search coverage.
- **Date range:** 1815-1900, overlapping the full target period.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Civil War (1861-1865) falls within the target period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are held at the National Archives; this survey's tools did not return a Schuylkill-specific military collection.
- **Where held:** NARA; state adjutant general records at Pennsylvania state archives (generic FamilySearch Wiki page).

### Cemetery records
- This survey's tool results did not return specific Schuylkill cemetery collections or coverage; not confirmed.

### Newspaper records
- Not confirmed by any tool result in this survey; local coal-region papers of the period (e.g. covering the Molly Maguires trials) are referenced generically by the FamilySearch Wiki Schuylkill County Genealogy page but no specific title or date range was returned.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia, the stated port of arrival for many Famine-era Irish immigrants to the coal region (FamilySearch Wiki).
- **Record types:** The Naturalization Records volume above; passenger lists are held at NARA.
- **Content note:** Examine full manifests - children travelling with parents are listed even as infants.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania state assessor ledgers, triennial from 1853, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity (FamilySearch Wiki, Coal Region Records page). Also "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" (Ancestry, via external_links_search) - predates the 1860-1900 target window but useful for family land context.
- **Substitute value:** Fills gaps around the lost 1890 census and between enumerations.

### Other record types
- **Colliery employment/Molly Maguires:** Company payroll ledgers for several Schuylkill collieries are held by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (FamilySearch Wiki, Schuylkill County Genealogy page). Molly Maguires trial transcripts, depositions and Pinkerton reports name hundreds of Irish-born miners and families (same page) - a distinctly rich, if adversarial, source for Irish coal-region research in the 1860s-1870s.
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898:** ~41,000 colliery worker entries (occupation, wage rate, parish of origin where stated) drawn from payroll books, but this index covers the lower anthracite field (Luzerne/Lackawanna), not Schuylkill's own collieries (FamilySearch Wiki, Coal Region Records page).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (982,415 persons); "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (person_count 0, not indexed) | Church Records volume gap (German-language, browse-only) and Probate gap | Free |
| Ancestry | "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/); "1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) | Pre-1860 tax/land gap; supplements the federal census series | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 5 volumes for Schuylkill, Pennsylvania in 1860-1900 with `complete: true`, i.e. the full matching set, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Colliery payroll ledgers for several collieries (FamilySearch Wiki) | Not stated by tool results; contact the society directly |
| Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic parish baptismal/marriage/burial registers for Schuylkill, 1860-1900 (FamilySearch Wiki) | Not stated by tool results; contact the archdiocesan archives |
| County courthouse (Schuylkill County) | Deed books, probate/court files, naturalization records (per volume_search coverage) | In-person / mail, per generic FamilySearch Wiki guidance |

## Records NOT online
- Colliery payroll ledgers at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County are not described by any tool result as digitized or online.
- Catholic parish registers held at the Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives are not described by any tool result as digitized or online for this period.
- Deed, probate, naturalization, marriage and church-record volumes identified by volume_search (imageGroupNumbers 007936749-007936753) are browse-only or only partially indexed images on FamilySearch, not full third-party-searchable online databases.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey states that Schuylkill County's vital, church, probate, land, or naturalization records were destroyed; catalog_search returned zero hits (a cataloguing gap) rather than a stated loss, and volume_search's results above show these series survive in some form.

## Research tips
- Distinguish company payroll indexes (which name individual colliery workers) from mine-inspection and accident reports (organized by colliery, not by person) - FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- For an Irish ancestor who worked collieries in the lower anthracite field (Luzerne/Lackawanna) as well as Schuylkill, also check the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898 (~41,000 entries with occupation, wage rate, and parish of origin) - FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- Molly Maguires-related court records, depositions and Pinkerton reports name hundreds of Irish miners and their families in Schuylkill County during the 1860s-1870s - FamilySearch Wiki, [Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires).
- Search Catholic parish registers at the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not a Scranton or Allentown diocesan archive, for a Schuylkill ancestor in 1860-1900 - FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- The four generic FamilySearch Wiki place-page sections fetched for Pennsylvania/Schuylkill in this survey returned only boilerplate with no jurisdiction-specific content - treat Pennsylvania-specific vital-record start dates and research strategy as unconfirmed rather than assuming the generic page's absence of detail means no records exist.
- This survey covers Schuylkill County only; Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland and Carbon Counties (also in the anthracite region) still need their own locality-guide surveys.

# Locality Guide: Vermont, United States (Pre-statehood, approx. 1749–1791)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** Vermont was not a formally organized jurisdiction in this period. It was disputed territory claimed by both New York and New Hampshire (the "New Hampshire Grants"), governed as an independent republic ("Vermont Republic") from 1777 until admitted as the 14th U.S. state in 1791 (FamilySearch Wiki, "Vermont Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Disputed between the Province of New York and the Province of New Hampshire before and during the Vermont Republic period; became the State of Vermont in 1791.

## Boundary Changes
- Vermont was claimed concurrently by New York and New Hampshire through the mid-18th century; grantees under New Hampshire's land grants ("New Hampshire Grants") were often not recognized by New York, producing disputed-claim records.
- Vermont operated as a self-declared independent republic from 1777 to 1791, before formal admission as a state.
- Because jurisdiction was contested and unsettled for the whole target period, records of land and governance from this era may be found filed under **New York or New Hampshire** provincial authority as well as under Vermont/"Grants" record-keeping — search all three when tracing a family here before 1791.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in **1857** (FamilySearch Wiki, "Vermont Genealogy") — decades after the target period.
- **What exists for the pre-statehood era:** Some town clerk records survive unevenly back to the 1770s.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices directly; no digitized/online location for these town-level records was confirmed by the tools used in this survey.
- **Gaps:** No statewide pre-1857 vital registration; coverage for the 1770s–1791 window depends entirely on which town clerks' records survive.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers, family Bibles, early town clerk books, and the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (below) as an indirect resident list.

### Land Records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds, organized by township grant.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Grants were originally issued under New Hampshire's colonial authority; New York, as the competing claimant, refused to recognize many of them.
- **Key record — Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** Prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood, enumerating roughly **1,800 grantees** of the disputed New Hampshire grants, with grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. Per the FamilySearch Wiki, this is "the earliest systematic resident list for the future state."
- **Where held:** No specific digitized or cataloged holding location was confirmed in this survey — collections_search, volume_search, and catalog_search returned zero hits for Vermont in this period.

### Town Histories (as a Record Substitute)
- Nineteenth-century Vermont town histories, mostly published 1860–1900, **reprint colonial-era proprietors' records** that are otherwise difficult to access (FamilySearch Wiki, "Vermont Genealogy"). For the pre-statehood period, these published histories may be the most practical substitute for lost or scattered original proprietors' records.

### Census Records
- The first federal decennial census (1790) falls at the very tail end of the pre-statehood period — effectively after, not within, most of this research window.

### Church, Probate, Court, Military, Cemetery, Tax Records
- None of these record types returned Vermont-specific, period-specific content in this survey's tool searches. This is a **confirmed coverage gap in this survey**, not evidence these records never existed. Researchers should contact Vermont town and county historical societies and the Vermont State Archives directly for proprietors' records, church registers, and early court minutes.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | What It Covers | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (Vermont Genealogy Wiki) | General guidance; no Vermont pre-1857 specific holdings confirmed by tools | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records — relevant for the Revolutionary War era within this window | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records, where town clerk vital records are absent | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (relevant only after 1790) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal-level records (post-1790 census, later military/pension files) | Free (research) |

> **Important caveat:** `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and `catalog_search` each returned **zero matches** for Vermont for 1770–1791. This means no FamilySearch-indexed collections, digitized volumes, or catalog entries specific to Vermont for this period could be confirmed in this survey — not that none exist. Plan on physical/archival research rather than assuming online indexing will surface pre-statehood material.

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont town clerk offices | Early town vital records (some from the 1770s) | In-person or written request to the town |
| Vermont State Archives | Presumed custodian of state-level materials | Contact directly (not independently confirmed by tool results) |
| Local historical societies | Proprietors' records, church registers, early court minutes | Varies |

---

## Records NOT Online (Confirmed Gaps)
- The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule's digital/physical holding location was not identified by any tool in this survey.
- Pre-1857 town clerk vital records are described by the FamilySearch Wiki as surviving "unevenly," with no online aggregation confirmed — consult town clerks directly.
- Church records, probate, court, and tax records for pre-statehood Vermont returned no FamilySearch collection, volume, or catalog hits.

## Known Record Losses
- No tool result specifically confirmed a documented record destruction event (e.g., courthouse fire) for pre-statehood Vermont. The uneven survival noted by the Wiki reflects the informal governance of the era rather than a confirmed destruction event.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search under all three jurisdictions.** Because Vermont was claimed by both New York and New Hampshire before 1791, pre-statehood records may be filed under any of the three jurisdictional names. The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule itself was created under New York colonial authority to adjudicate New Hampshire grants — a clear sign that records crossed jurisdictional lines.

2. **Identify the specific town first.** The 1857 statewide civil-registration start date is the key dividing line. Before that year, everything depends on which town clerk's books survive, so pinpoint the town before searching further.

3. **Mine town histories.** Nineteenth-century Vermont town histories (mostly 1860–1900) routinely reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are hard to access elsewhere — these are among the most useful sources for the pre-statehood period.

4. **Plan for archival, not online, research.** Because online tools found no indexed or digitized Vermont collections for this era, the realistic research path runs through town clerks, local historical societies, and the Vermont State Archives rather than online databases.

5. **Check Revolutionary War military records.** The 1777–1791 Vermont Republic period overlaps with the American Revolution; Fold3 and NARA pension files may document men who served from Vermont territory during this window.

---

*This guide covers Vermont for the years before statehood (1791), when it was disputed frontier territory claimed by both New York and New Hampshire and governed loosely as the independent "Vermont Republic." The clearest surviving record from this era is the 1771 land-grant list of about 1,800 settlers, plus scattered town clerk books and later town histories reprinting old land records. Most research for this window will require physical town and archival sources rather than online search.*
